The Resilience of Self-reliance in China: Autonomy, Interdependence and Order-shaping
abstract: The idea of “self-reliance” has endured in Chinese political discourse for nearly a century, transcending profound changes in China’s political, economic and strategic circumstances. Although it is frequently misinterpreted as economic isolation or autarky, the idea of self-reliance in China has always acknowledged the country’s engagement with the global economy. Drawing on the discursive institutionalist concept of ideational resilience, we show that self-reliance comprises three interlocking elements: autonomy, interdependence and order-shaping. While these sit in tension with one another, they have also accommodated one another since the earliest articulations of the idea. This tripartite structure has enabled Chinese leaders since the Republican era to reinterpret and usefully deploy the idea of self-reliance. Our findings underscore the resilience of Chinese foreign economic policy ideas, as well as the ideational logic behind Xi Jinping’s seemingly contradictory pursuit of technological self-reliance, open global markets and greater connectivity with the developing world.

title: Ideology Without Unity: The Rhizomatic Logic of Xi Jinping Thought
abstract: This article reconceptualizes Xi Jinping Thought on Socialism with Chinese Characteristics (Xi Thought hereafter) not as a coherent doctrine but as a rhizomatic ideological formation. Drawing on the work of Gilles Deleuze and Félix Guattari, it treats Xi Thought as a configuration in which coherence is not presupposed but produced through the continual recombining of fragments across institutional sites. Based on an analysis of official publications, including collected works, excerpt volumes and study readers, the article shows how Xi’s speeches are disassembled and reassembled across domains such as law, economy, diplomacy and culture. These recompositions render ideology modular and resilient, allowing elements to be activated, re-weighted or sidelined without destabilizing the system as a whole. The article further argues that ideological coherence is generated through distributed and compulsory participation by Party and state actors, who are required to embed fragments of Xi Thought into institutional practice. Conceptualizing Xi Thought as a rhizome shifts analysis from doctrinal meaning to the operational logic through which ideology acquires administrative force within the Chinese party-state.

title: Bureaucratic Restructuring and the State-led (De-)Financialization of Local Governance in China
abstract: State-led financialization has emerged as a salient feature of local governance in China, yet it remains underexplored through the lens of bureaucratic restructuring. This paper traces the evolution of local financial agencies since 2002 through four distinct stages: local financial offices ( jinrongban ), financial bureaus ( jinrongju ), financial regulatory bureaus ( jinrong jianguanju ) and financial commissions ( jinrongwei ). Initially, local governments established jinrongban to harness financial capital for regional development. By proactively connecting local firms with capital markets to facilitate corporate listings, they embedded financial logic into local governance, reflecting local state-led financialization. Subsequently, the central government formalized these bodies into jinrongju with expanded mandates, deepening state-led financialization. Later, it systematically devolved regulatory responsibilities and renamed them jinrong jianguanju , elevating regulatory functions to a top priority, illustrating how the central government selectively steered the direction of financialization. Ultimately, provincial agencies were reorganized into jinrongwei and stripped of development functions, while city-level counterparts were largely closed, signifying a shift towards central state-led de-financialization. This trajectory was driven by shifting central–local dynamics, as early bottom-up initiatives were superseded by top-down control. The bureaucratic restructuring examined in this study offers new insights into the state-led (de-)financialization of local governance in China.

title: Explaining China’s High Welfare Spending: Local Models and Drivers of Fiscally Oriented Affordable Housing
abstract: While the world has been undergoing a global wave of welfare retrenchment since the turn of the 21st century, China’s spending on welfare provision has grown remarkably. Through a comparative study of the public housing provision programmes in two districts within the same municipality, this paper explores models of fiscally oriented public housing provision and their underlying driving forces. Drawing on data from archives, interviews and intensive fieldwork conducted in south-west China from 2014 to 2018, we identify two prominent public housing models: the entrepreneurial model and the extractive model. We propose that the choice of different welfare provision approaches is linked to local fiscal pressures and the target responsibility system. This paper sheds light on the structure of political incentives within China’s local governments in relation to public service provision and explores how local leaders improve public welfare in a non-Western setting.

title: Governing through Visibility: Local Government Experimentation with Internet Celebrity Cities in China
abstract: The rise of internet celebrity cities has become one of the most striking phenomena in China since 2021. How do local governments respond and harness this trend to advance their development goals? This study focuses on local experimentation in creating such cities, drawing on the case of the Village Football Super League ( Cun chao 村超) in Guizhou. We identify policy entrepreneurship as a key driver of local experimentation and highlight three core strategies for creating internet celebrity cities: crafting local symbols, co-producing viral content and mitigating public opinion risk. Further analysis shows that this experimentation, by attracting massive public attention, simultaneously promotes economic growth, strengthens social cohesion, reinforces state narratives and projects China’s national image onto the global stage. Overall, the findings suggest an emerging model in which public attention becomes a core resource for local development and governance in China’s digital era.

title: From Contention to Clientelism: Evidence from the Ten-Year Fishing Ban in China
abstract: How do ordinary Chinese people circumvent unpopular state policies? The existing literature primarily focuses on resistance against local bureaucrats. Drawing on ethnographic research on the ten-year fishing ban in the Yangtze River Basin, this article finds that fishermen (clients) continue to fish by maintaining patron–client relationships with the enforcers of the fishing ban (patrons). Ordinary fishermen seek the protection of enforcers through bribery. Enhanced state monitoring under the fishing ban facilitates bribery-based clientelism by weakening the fishermen’s everyday resistance, but it also constrains the power of enforcers by increasing the risk that their corruption will be discovered by upper-level authorities. For extremely poor fishermen, who are barely able to afford to pay bribes, their daily acts of resistance are morally justified by the need for subsistence safety, presenting enforcers with a dilemma: they must fulfil their law enforcement duties while also ensuring the survival of these individuals to maintain social stability. Therefore, cultivating a clientelist relationship with impoverished fishermen enables enforcers to manage their noncompliance, thereby balancing these conflicting goals. While clientelism protects people from unpopular policies to some extent, it more fundamentally strengthens the power of local bureaucrats, creating the potential for greater exploitation and larger-scale popular grievances in the long run.

title: Promoting Meritocracy through Recognition: The Post-recognition Career Trajectories of China’s Model County Party Secretaries
authors: Weilin Xiao; Haoyue Hu; Cai (Vera) Zuo
abstract: The increasingly proactive role of central authority in managing subprovincial leaders is understudied and our understanding of the function of political recognition in contemporary China remains inadequate. By adopting an expanded view of political meritocracy and using difference-in-differences analysis of original data about China’s model county Party secretaries, we demonstrate the ramifications of political recognition in generating a merit-based fast track and find that the recognition of model county Party secretaries has a lasting positive impact on recipients’ subsequent career advancement, although this impact is uneven. These findings enhance our understanding of the role of centrally bestowed political honours in promoting meritocracy, the non-institutionalized soft measures in shaping political incentives and the central–local interaction in the dynamics of political recognition in contemporary China.

title: Solving Agency Problems in Chinese Universities: Academics in the Shadow of the Party’s Declared Leadership
abstract: How does the party-state exercise leadership over universities and manage the individuals embedded in the university system without restraining their capacity for excellence and innovation? I argue that the presidential responsibility system has resolved a fundamental agency problem in Chinese universities. The system is supported by a set of mechanisms designed to enforce loyalty to the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party. It can easily adapt to political changes and thus maintain authoritarian rule without compromising the overarching agenda of research excellence.

title: Political Satire and the Decline of Discourse Quality: Evidence from China’s Online Public Sphere
abstract: Extensive research has examined whether political satire promotes or suppresses political discussion, but far less attention has been paid to how it shapes discourse quality. This study investigates the impact of political satire on discourse quality by scrutinizing the substance of online discussions in a non-democratic context. Drawing on manual content analysis of discussions on a major Chinese social media platform surrounding China’s controversial policy to raise the age of retirement, we analysed original posts and subsequent replies (N = 3,400) to assess the impact of satire on online political talk. The results show that political satire significantly decreases topic relevance and rationality, while exerting no significant effect on civility, and virtually precludes argument reciprocity. These findings contribute theoretically by shifting the focus from whether satire stimulates political engagement to how it influences the substantive quality of deliberation. They also invite a reassessment of the often-overemphasized optimistic role of political satire, highlighting its potential to erode rational and constructive discourse.

title: Desperate Acts of Democracy: Identity Threat, Autocratization and Voter Turnout in Hong Kong
authors: Lev Nachman; Nathan Kar Ming Chan; Chit Wai John Mok
abstract: How does identity threat affect mass political participation during times of autocratization? Building on social identity and group threat literatures, we theorize that perceived threats to Hong Konger identity increase voter turnout; however, the political salience of this threat is contingent on the degree of autocratization. We test this argument utilizing the case of Hong Kong, whose ongoing incorporation into the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has entered an unprecedented era of autocratization. We argue that threats to Hong Konger identity came to mobilize voter participation, especially as autocratization progressed in Hong Kong. Hong Kongers resisted during this period of political change through their intention to turn out to vote. We conducted three original experiments during different transitionary periods of Hong Kong’s autocratic shift. We find that priming identity threat had no effect on voter turnout before Hong Kong’s autocratic divergence. However, once more extreme forms of autocratization began, Hong Kongers assigned to an identical identity threat treatment were substantially more likely to report a higher likelihood of voting. This mobilizing effect persisted in a third experiment. Our results suggest a paradox where citizens’ propensity to vote increases when faced with perceived shrinking opportunities to participate in elections during times of authoritarian transition.

title: China’s Internal Security Spending: An Assessment of New Data
abstract: Internal security has been a governance priority under Xi Jinping. How does China’s budget reflect this prioritization? This research report presents updated data on China’s internal security spending, 1992–2022, revealing a mix of continuity and change. Domestic security expenditure continues to rise, more than doubling from 2012 to 2022, but has risen mostly in proportion to the People’s Republic of China’s overall expenditure. The balance between central and local expenditure has shifted further towards local spending, which, in the context of rising local fiscal constraint, may increase pressure on local public security bureaus. The Ministry of Public Security continues to receive the largest share of domestic security spending, while the proportion of internal security spending allocated to the People’s Armed Police (PAP) has decreased, probably reflecting the reorganization of the PAP in 2017–2018. Spending per capita and relative to GDP continues to be higher in locations that are politically sensitive, including Beijing, Tibet and Xinjiang.

title: Discovering Controversies through Reversions: A Text-based Analysis of China’s Two-phase Bill Changes
abstract: This study uncovers hidden disputes in China’s law-making process by systematically tracking bill changes across executive and legislative phases. Utilizing an original dataset of 45 executive-initiated bills (2008–2023), it identifies a consistent pattern of reversions – instances where executive-approved changes to draft bills were overridden in the legislature – revealing the National People’s Congress to be a key policy battleground. Reversions are concentrated in bills concerning health, safety and environment, often involving scope, regulatory frameworks and legal liability. Combined with qualitative case studies, these findings demonstrate the legislature’s crucial role in facilitating monitoring and negotiation in the policy process, offering new insights into executive–legislative dynamics in China’s single-party regime.

title: How the Chinese Public Perceives South-East Asia: Affinity, Annoyance and Apprehension
abstract: This article explores how the Chinese public perceives South-East Asia. Using original survey data collected in China, it suggests three perceptual frames. The “affinity” frame, which is rooted in historical Chinese migration and diaspora ties, generates feelings of kinship and cultural connection. Conversely, the “annoyance” frame stems from contemporary geopolitical tensions, particularly South China Sea disputes, where several South-East Asian countries are viewed as provocateurs challenging China’s regional authority. The “apprehension” frame characterizes the region as exotic yet dangerous, a perception reinforced by recent cyber scams and criminal activities targeting Chinese citizens, creating stereotypes of South-East Asia as lawless and unsafe. The article analyses the survey data for the statistical distribution of these frames and discusses their political implications. By exploring how historical ties, geopolitical tensions and security concerns simultaneously shape Chinese public opinion, the article illuminates the complex perceptual landscape that may influence China’s diplomatic and economic relations with South-East Asia.

title: Forever Hong Kong: A Global City’s Decolonization Struggle Ching Kwan Lee. Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2025. 344 pp. £37.95 (hbk). ISBN 9780674290198
abstract: Forever Hong Kong offers a bold reinterpretation of the city's contentious political trajectory from the handover era to the present.The book is masterfully written and meticulously researched.It is a unique and valuable contribution to Hong Kong studies and beyond.Lee's core question is how Hong Kongers transformed from "colonized subjects" complacent with the status quo into "decolonizing subjects" willing to take action and chart their own history.Her answer is that Hong Kong's successive waves of contention -from the 2003 Article 23 protests through the 2014 Umbrella Movement to the 2019 Anti-Extradition movement -are best understood as a decolonization struggle, rather than a conventional fight for democratization.The colonialism to be unravelled, she argues, was not purely British.It was a "double coloniality" co-produced by London and Beijing, held together by four interlocking "colonial myths" that constrained Hong Kongers' political agency and imagination: stability and prosperity, free-market capitalism, rule of law, and China as destiny.The first chapter reconstructs how each pillar was manufactured and hardened into common sense; the rest of the book traces how various political and economic ruptures pushed activists and ordinary citizens to challenge each pillar in turn, culminating in the 2019 uprising that Lee calls both "the peak of the city's ongoing decolonization struggle decades in the making and the opening salvo of a new era of confrontation between Western neoliberal capitalism and Chinese state capitalism" (p.2).The book's empirical depth is impressive.Lee draws on ethnographic fieldwork from 2019 through 2023, in-depth interviews with a wide cross-section of participants -from frontline militants and student leaders to bankers, medics, accountants and diaspora organizers -as well as archival materials and intellectual writings.Chapters four and five provide particularly illuminating details about militant frontline protesters and the international front, which had remained obscure to outsiders.By recasting Hong Kong's political history as a quest for decolonization, Lee offers a refreshing perspective.Most scholarship on Hong Kong's politics -including much of my own -works within contentious politics or democratization theory, privileging topics such as hybrid regimes, electoral authoritarianism, opportunity structures and repertoire shifts.These works focus on both structure and dynamics: what explains protest participation, how movements escalate and how political opportunities open and close.Lee poses a different question: how did people come to understand what they were doing, and why?The payoff is most visible in her analysis of protest violence.While contentious politics scholars tend to explain radicalization through state repression and organizational dynamics, Lee reconstructs how "brave warriors" themselves theorized and negotiated the use of violence.These accounts capture emotional, ethical and calculative dimensions that analyses on structure and dynamics tend to flatten.

Managing Hydro-dependence and Risk: Hong Kong’s Water Insurance Policy, 1967–1982
abstract: Using archival and unofficial sources, this article examines how political calculations, economic considerations, local consumption patterns and international dynamics shaped the colonial administration’s water governance strategies in Hong Kong. It focuses on how the 1967 water emergency prompted the colonial government to recalibrate its approach, from a policy of manageable dependency to one of risk aversion. After 1967, an “insurance policy” ensuring a “basic ration” was pursued. This led to the construction of the Lok On Pai desalination plant. The article then traces developments from 1976 to 1982, when Hong Kong gradually moved to a regionally integrated strategy, driven not only by improved Sino-British relations but also by economic considerations, growing public intolerance of water rationing and the Middle East oil crisis. By 1982, Hong Kong’s water insurance policy had officially ended; Chinese water was classified as “reliable.” By exploring these understudied developments and factors, the article contributes to the histories of water management, colonial Hong Kong and China.

Balancing Accommodation and Authority: Husbands’ Family Strategies in Transnational Marriages in North-East China
abstract: This article examines South–South transnational marriages between Vietnamese women and Chinese men in North-East China, focusing on the strategies husbands’ families employ to sustain these unions. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of family strategies and in-depth interviews with 26 households, it develops a “departure-restraint” framework to explain how receiving families respond to the persistent possibility of a bride’s marital exit. The findings show that these strategies rest on a balance between limited accommodation and selective authority: Vietnamese brides are granted a degree of autonomy in everyday matters, while husbands’ families retain control over major household decisions. The article further argues that the relatively narrow economic gap between sending and receiving regions in South–South marriages reshapes household dynamics in distinctive ways. Under conditions of limited economic opportunity, husbands’ families maintain marital stability not through outright domination, but through calibrated negotiations over everyday autonomy and household authority.

title: Feminized Revival: Han Chinese Dress, Gender and Cultural Nationalism in Contemporary China
abstract: Women hold disproportionate authority in China’s contemporary Hanfu revival, where Han-ness operates through implicit cultural codes rather than explicit ethnic claims. Recent scholarship highlights how Han-ness circulates as a moral, etiquette-centred grammar of “proper culture.” Drawing on 18 months of ethnography across six sites in China, this article shows how gender mediates that grammar and shapes the performances of Han-ness. Women, as arbiters of taste and propriety, enact an assertive banal nationalism through aesthetic and organizational labour. Men, marginal within the field, perform defensive overt nationalism through didactic historical narratives and moralized claims to legitimacy. To explain this pattern of identity formation and boundary making, I advance the notion of gendered everyday nationhood. The article contributes to scholarship on nationalism by showing how embodied practices sustain national belonging, and how mundane evaluation and boundary policing reproduce nationhood in everyday life.

title: The Origins of Land Finance: Local Resistance and Top-Down Imposition
abstract: Land sales have been a significant source of revenue for Chinese local governments since the early 2000s. Contrary to popular belief, local governments did not turn to land finance to make up for lost tax revenues after the 1994 tax sharing reform. Rather, both before and after 1994, corrupt land sales were widespread, as officials sold land far below market prices in return for bribes. Even as the fiscal incentives for local governments to adopt land finance increased in the 1990s, state agents continued acting on their own personal interests rather than the institutional interests of local governments. Local governments only began to sell land at higher, market prices when an anti-corruption campaign launched by the central government made doing so a political imperative in the early 2000s. Local governments were much more responsive to political imperatives than to fiscal incentives.

title: Subversive Amplification: Online Dissent and the Limits of Information Control in China
abstract: Intensified information control severely constrains digital contention in China, yet online mass events occasionally occur. Using a dataset of 274,721 Weibo messages, this study examines mobilization, coordination and grievance articulation during a two-day episode of online dissent in the aftermath of the 2022 Urumqi residential building fire, which preceded the White Paper protests. It argues that users were activated by public communication failures that transformed manifold grievances into outrage, and that the associated hashtags provided anchors to which criticism could be attached. In a process this study terms “subversive amplification,” concentrated engagement amplified the hashtags’ visibility, and with it the critical content attached to them. However, absent the unifying function of opinion leaders, grievance articulation remained fragmented and did not converge on unified demands. The case illustrates the inherent vulnerabilities of information control but also the conditions and limits of their exploitation.

title: Rising Engagement and Substantive Responsiveness: 13 Years of Online Petitioning in China
abstract: The Chinese government has invested heavily in online petition platforms to channel public grievances, yet systematic longitudinal evidence on citizen–state interactions within these venues remains limited. This research report presents nationwide evidence showing that both public participation and government responsiveness through e-petition institutions have increased markedly since Xi Jinping took office. Analysing more than four million citizen appeals submitted to the country’s largest online petition portal, Message Board for Leaders, from January 2011 to January 2024, we find a twelvefold rise in petition volume and a fivefold increase in users, largely driven by urban residents in eastern provinces. Appeals have also diversified, with notable growth in housing-related issues and more strategic appeals directed at Party secretaries. Meanwhile, local governments have raised response rates from 50 per cent to 98 per cent, shortened average wait times from 176 to 19 days, and increased the substantive resolution rate from 17 per cent to 31 per cent over the past decade.

Ideology, Memory, and Silence: Thai Studies under Cold War Historiography in China
abstract: Between the 1950s and 1970s, the People’s Republic of China (PRC) maintained contact and cooperation with the Communist Party of Thailand (CPT) through multiple channels. The CPT received material support, political training, and ideological guidance from China, particularly from bases in Yunnan Province. Using the development of Thai Studies in China as a case study, this article examines how Chinese academia has engaged with—or avoided—the Cold War history of Thailand. Through a critical review of the field, it identifies structural tensions shaped by political sensitivity and institutional constraints, situating these dynamics within the broader context of Southeast Asian studies. Such constraints influence topic selection, access to sources, and publication practices, resulting in a field characterized by narrowed perspectives, uneven critical engagement, and structurally constrained academic autonomy. In this sense, Thai Studies in China reflects a paradoxical trajectory in which the field has been repeatedly shaped, disrupted, and revived by shifting political imperatives rather than by autonomous scholarly inquiry.

title: Learning in (Re)Production: Spare-time Learning and the Reproduction of Gendered Labor in Socialist China
abstract: This article examines spare-time learning (yèyú xuéxí) in socialist China as a form of labor-mediated pedagogical governance that expanded women’s access to education while simultaneously reproducing gendered divisions of labor. Drawing on archival materials from Shaanxi Province, I trace how spare-time learning was organized across urban industrial and rural agricultural settings, showing that it constituted an ambitious effort to democratize intellectual authority by locating knowledge production within collective labor practice. Yet the capacity of spare-time learning to serve as an equalizing institution was unevenly structured across institutional contexts. I introduce the concept of a “gendered mobility loop” to specify the mechanisms through which the gendered division of labor was continually reconstituted within socialist pedagogy. By tracing shifts from early literacy campaigns to increasingly moralized political training, I argue that women’s double burden was not merely a residual legacy of tradition or an effect of incomplete implementation but was continually reconstituted through pedagogical arrangements embedded in production regimes. Reconceptualizing spare-time learning as a site of ideological reproduction embedded in production, this article contributes to feminist scholarship on social reproduction under socialism and to Marxist cultural studies of the education–labor nexus.

title: Hidden Smoke: Air Pollution, Agrarian Change, and Governance Gaps in Luang Prabang, Laos
abstract: Air pollution has emerged as a major public health and economic threat in Southeast Asia, yet Laos has received limited attention in scholarly and policy debates despite significant mortality and economic losses. This article analyses the drivers, lived experiences, and governance of air pollution in Luang Prabang, Laos’ premier tourist destination and a UNESCO World Heritage city. Drawing on semi-structured interviews, field observations, and satellite data, our findings challenge dominant policy narratives that attribute haze primarily to traditional swidden cultivation. Instead, commercial agrarian change, particularly cassava expansion, grass cultivation, and cattle pasture expansion linked to regional and Chinese cattle demand and a prolonged urban landfill fire, drove air pollution in 2023. These sources stem from labor shortages, economic insecurity, poor urban waste planning, and a reliance on fire as a low-cost management tool. Despite significant health, livelihood, and tourism impacts, haze remains underappreciated and underfunded. Weak monitoring infrastructure, fragmented institutional responsibilities, and the absence of disaggregated health data render air pollution uncertain and socially normalized. The article argues that air pollution in Luang Prabang represents a form of slow violence, maintained by epistemic gaps and administrative silence within a development model that prioritizes expanded agriculture and tourism over environmental protection.

title: Telling What was not Told: Acehnese Women’s Narratives of Conflict and the Tsunami
authors: Alfi Rahman; Rizanna Rosemary; Safrina; Norma Susanti; Syahrul Ridha; Siti Ghaisani Mastura; Nada Nafira Almanzani
abstract: This study investigates how Acehnese women experience, remember, and transmit narratives about prolonged armed conflict and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami. In-depth interviews were conducted with women across two generational categories: those who had directly experienced these events (experiential narrators) and those who have learned the stories through familial or community transmission (post-memory narrators). The study situates narratives as a social practice, exploring how women’s experiences, survival, and resilience are interpreted, negotiated, and passed on. The study reveals a striking divergence in how these two crises are remembered and narrated. The tsunami, often seen as a divine test, has been spiritualized, moralized, and publicly commemorated through museums, school drills, and religious discourse. This structured and didactic form of storytelling fosters intergenerational compassion and preparedness. In contrast, conflict memories are fraught with moral complexity, silence, and fear. These narratives, often fragmented, emotionally restrained, and selectively told, have been shaped by past surveillance, suspicion, and unresolved trauma. The study underscores the importance of integrating women-centered approaches into post-disaster and post-conflict recovery. It also shows how the recognition and protection of women’s voices is vital to understanding long-term resilience, collective memory, and processes of social repair.

title: Technocratic Turn: Authoritarianism, Global Capitalism, and Cambodia’s State Transformation since 2013
abstract: Scholars have characterized Cambodia as a weak state, strong party governance system in which administrative institutions are subordinated to the ruling Cambodian People’s Party (CPP). This article argues that since 2013 Cambodian governance has taken a significant technocratic turn, as party rule has become increasingly dependent on a stronger and more capable administrative state. It traces a reform pattern involving selective creation and upgrading of institutional nodes that expand overall state administrative capacity without disrupting the party-political order. Through three cases — the transformation of the National Bank of Cambodia through the Bakong digital payment system, the restructuring of public–private partnership frameworks to fund the Techo International Airport, and the creation of executive-linked agencies such as the Techo Startup Center — the article shows how new centers of administrative capacity have emerged and been positioned at the core of the state’s developmental agenda. These institutions have enhanced the party-state’s capacity to mobilize revenue, coordinate and develop mega infrastructures, and formalize the economy, producing a more capable but still party-embedded state. The Cambodian case illustrates a particular trajectory within broader contemporary developmental state-making under global capitalism, in which strengthened administrative states and political authoritarianism are mutually reinforcing.

title: The Making of an Indian Company Town: Manufactured Cosmopolitanism, Communal Violence, and Urban Memory in Jamshedpur, India
abstract: In 1907, after months of prospecting across India, the little-known and remote hamlet of Sakchi in Singhbhum was chosen by Jamshetji Nusserwanji Tata (1839-1904), founder of the Tata Group, as the location for India’s first indigenously owned iron and steel works. This paper examines the construction of an institutional cultural memory of what would become the planned city of Jamshedpur as an integral part of India’s industrial heritage, steeped in ideas of progress, modernity and cosmopolitanism. The article juxtaposes this cultural memory with the lived experiences and memories of Jamshedpur inhabitants who have witnessed its transformation in response to and beyond the institutional narrative of the ideal steel city. Finally, the article discusses the immediate and long-term impacts of communal riots in 1964 and 1979 and the ways in which this violence is remembered or forgotten. In doing so, the article argues that public and private histories and memories of Jamshedpur intersect, overlap, and negotiate with each other in ways that complicate and contradict a carefully cultivated discourse of model industrial urbanism that has been erected on a foundation of manufactured cosmopolitanism.

title: Reproducing Patriarchy Through Women’s Proxy Representation in Local Governments: An Ethnographic Perspective from Rural Punjab, Pakistan
abstract: This article examines how Pakistan's local government gender quota policy, aimed at improving women's political representation, has been undermined by entrenched patriarchal structures in rural Punjab. Based on longitudinal ethnographic research, including fieldwork conducted in 2005-2006 and 2019, with follow-up observations in 2024, the study highlights the problem of proxy representation. In this scenario, elected women often act as figurehead councilors while their male relatives wield actual decision-making power. The analysis indicates that the apparent increase in female representation often amounts to mere symbolic inclusion, offering little genuine empowerment for women. By drawing on feminist theories of representation and agency, along with concepts of patriarchal bargains and a governmentality perspective, the article argues that state-led “empowerment” reforms can be co-opted and reshaped by local kinship norms concerning honor and authority. In practice, rather than fundamentally disrupting male dominance, Pakistan’s gender quota has largely been transformed into a new form of patriarchy—one that maintains male control while creating a façade of female representation. These findings contribute to discussions on feminist governance by illustrating that efforts to democratize gender relations must confront deeply entrenched social structures.

title: Seeing Like a Colonial State: Post-colonial Dossierism, Patriarchal Governance, and Indigenous Status Recognition in Taiwan
abstract: When I applied for Truku Indigenous status in 2022, I discovered that my mother had never been officially registered as Indigenous in Taiwan and my application was therefore denied. Only through an arduous bureaucratic process was I able to obtain state recognition of my Truku Indigenous identity. This experience led me to ask what epistemic and ideological foundations structure Taiwan’s Indigenous Peoples Status Act (IPSA). Drawing on narrative inquiry and combining autoethnographic reflection with legal and policy analysis, this article identifies two ideologies underlying the Act: post-colonial dossierism and patriarchal governance. Taiwan’s recognition regime privileges colonial archives over Indigenous self-determination while operating through patriarchal norms of descent and identity transmission. This study contributes to the literature on postcolonialism in two ways. First, it identifies dossierism and patriarchal governance as mechanisms through which colonial epistemology is reproduced in law. Second, it shows that once colonially produced documents are codified as mandatory state law, it legitimized the colonial way of seeing and, in turn, shapes how colonized subjects come to understand themselves.

title: Indigenous Communities and Development: The Mising People and Dam Construction in Assam, India
abstract: Much of the early literature on dams and Indigenous peoples focused on resistance and organized opposition to the projects, with an emphasis on threats to Indigenous life ways, sustainability, and their roles as custodians of nature. However, more recent scholarship highlights the complex ways in which affected populations respond to such projects. This article examines how Indigenous people in one community in Northeast India engage with a development project that dispossesses them, provoking opposition to the project, while also offering opportunities to enter the market economy and earn higher incomes. It discusses the case of the Subansiri Lower Hydro Electric Project (SLHEP) in Assam. The article argues that what appears to be a contradiction in how people respond to this project reflects a more complex response to the set of changes brought about by a growing neoliberal order and the place that Indigenous working people find themselves in. This is marked by the rapid erosion of the material life worlds of Indigenous peoples and a growing dependence on market interactions for meeting most basic needs, alongside growing aspirations and the precarity brought on by a crisis of social reproduction.

title: Under Construction: Frontier Infrastructure in Northeast India
abstract: This article investigates encounters between infrastructure projects and Indigenous communities in Northeast India. Focusing on two projects by the National Hydroelectric Power Corporation in the Dollungmukh region of Arunachal Pradesh, namely the Subansiri Lower Hydroelectric Project (SLHEP) and a Nyder Namlo (prayer hall), it shows how a large-scale, long-drawn-out construction process has become the turf for intense encounters between local communities, the state, and infrastructural technologies. Projects such as these function as a form of infrastructural optics, through which the state materially and discursively manifests itself and thereby constantly reaffirms and adjusts the material and discursive scaffolding of this frontier region. Based on ethnographic fieldwork, the article demonstrates how the construction of the SLHEP, one of India’s largest dams, has reshaped the local political economy, aspirations, and social relations. The article also highlights how the Nyder Namlo serves as a critical convergence point where state-making and efforts to undergird the collective life of local communities blend through the construction regime across multiple material and discursive realms.

title: Governing Social Change in Amdo: Deficit Ideologies, Educational Desire, and the Depoliticization of Tibetan Education
abstract: Tibetan education in the People’s Republic of China (PRC) has received international attention and criticism in recent years as an issue of colonial boarding schools that aim to assimilate young Tibetans. The proliferation of state-run boarding schools was the outcome of a central government policy of school consolidation, presented as a new panacea for the problems of rural education, and which resulted in the closure of hundreds of thousands of schools across the PRC. Drawing on ethnographic fieldwork in 2012–2013 and 2024 in parts of the Amdo region of Tibet (now part of Qinghai and Gansu Provinces), this article examines how education policies and practices are mobilized discursively as technical, practical, and non-political, while simultaneously extending state power into the everyday lives of rural Tibetans with cross-generational disciplinary effects. Contestation has been mitigated by existing and new forms of educational desire, while education has been “depoliticized” by quality discourses and deficit ideologies – including by some Tibetan educators – in the context of rapid socio-economic change and precarity.

title: Green Star over Thailand: Esperanto and Leftist Internationalism in the Thai Chinese Community during the 1930s
abstract: This article examines the Esperanto movement within the Thai Chinese community during the 1930s as a prism through which to explore the early formation of leftist internationalism in Thailand. Drawing on a diverse corpus of primary sources, this study reconstructs how a small but committed group of intellectuals mobilized Esperanto as both a practical tool for transnational communication and a symbolic vehicle for articulating a vision of leftist internationalism grounded in the specific realities of China’s anti-Japanese resistance. The article argues that the Esperanto movement was a transnational leftist cultural network that mediated the interplay between internationalism, nationalism, and communism—three forces that collectively shaped the political consciousness of Thai Chinese. The movement’s trajectory reveals both the possibilities and vulnerabilities of such transnational projects. While ultimately crushed by the rise of Thai state nationalism under the Phibun Songkhram regime, the movement’s radical ideas and networks survived through clandestine channels. By tracing how Esperantists adapted internationalist discourse to serve China’s national salvation, this article illuminates a neglected chapter in Thai radicalism and contributes to broader efforts to decenter Eurocentric narratives of leftist internationalism by attending to the experiences of Southeast Asian diasporic communities.

title: Fear Politics and the Construction of Political Enemies: The Democratic Action Party and Malay-Islamic Narratives in Post-2018 Malaysia
abstract: This article examines how Malaysia’s Democratic Action Party (DAP) has been discursively constructed as a political adversary by rival Malay-Muslim political parties and nationalist actors in post-2018 Malaysia. Moving beyond static narratives of ethnic politics, it argues that portrayals of the DAP as a threat to Malay-Muslim interests do not reflect a fixed ideological order, but rather emerge from ongoing struggles over meaning, legitimacy, and political power. Drawing on a qualitative analysis of political speeches, media narratives, and digital discourse between 2018 and 2025, the article demonstrates how fear operates as a central mechanism in shaping political perceptions and mobilizing support. Rather than indicating a unified Malay response, these narratives are received unevenly across class, generational, and ideological lines, thereby revealing significant internal contestations. By focusing on political discourse, the article examines how political fear operates in practice. It contends that contemporary Malay-centric party politics are more accurately understood through a competitive and fragmented field of competing narratives.

title: Lee Siew Choh and His Discontents: Maoism and the Factionalization of Singapore’s Progressive Left after Operation Coldstore
abstract: This article explores how Maoism shaped, and was shaped by, the factionalization of Singapore’s progressive left and its flagship political party, the Barisan Sosialis (Socialist Front) after Operation Coldstore on February 2, 1963. Focusing especially on the Cultural Revolution period, it traces the emergence of Maoism in the city-state to texts and ideas from the People’s Republic of China that circulated widely within left-wing circles in Singapore starting in the 1950s, as well as to the three years after Coldstore, when Maoism came to dominate public leftist discourse and practice in Singapore. The article intervenes in the historiography of global Maoism by triangulating between the work of orthodox scholars such as Yinghong Cheng and recent, left-historical interpretations by the likes of Matthew Galway and Fabio Lanza. By focusing on the increasingly extremist Barisan and its Maoist critics such as the student activist Li Xiquan, it shows, contrary to orthodox analyses, that Maoism in Singapore cannot be reduced to a purely foreign ideology, and was, rather, underpinned by the Barisan and its critics’ shared commitment to Malaya as an anticolonial project and adaptation of Maoism to fit local circumstances. Maoists were likewise capable of critical self-reflection, as left-historical scholarship contends and the example of Li Xiquan suggests. Yet, such scholarship fails to capture how fanaticism, mimicry, and emotion were constitutive of Maoist experiences in Singapore, and indeed how ideological commitments evolved over time in ways that underscore these aspects of Singapore Maoism.

Toward Divergence: Social Trends in Tomb Epitaphs During Liao, Song, and Jin China
abstract: This study presents a comprehensive view of middle-period China by focusing on excavated epitaphs from Liao, Song, and Jin tombs. It systematically examines the social backgrounds of epitaph users, compares their compositions across dynasties, and delineates societal trends in North and South China. Although the stratum of officials dominated the use of epitaphs across all dynasties, the overall social composition of epitaph users reveals divergences between northern and southern dynasties. The Liao displayed the strongest aristocratic traits, with a remarkable proportion of epitaphs belonging to upper-level Khitan nobles. The Northern Song exhibited meritocratic characteristics, with a considerable number of epitaphs belonging to scholar-officials and shi 士 literati. It also featured the most diverse backgrounds among non-literati elite users, some of whom were expressive in their epitaphs, suggesting a lively local society. The destructive wars of the early twelfth century deepened the North-South divide. In the North, under the Jin, Jurchen and Han Chinese elites turned away from the use of epitaphs. In the Southern Song, the literati predominated among burials with epitaphs, while non-literati elites became more silent compared to their Northern Song predecessors. Many new types of epitaphs emerged in the southeastern region, where Neo-Confucianism flourished. These may have served as a means for Neo-Confucians to express their intellectual identity. The variety of these epitaphs further signaled growing internal differentiation among literati users. This macro-level comparative research of excavated epitaphs illuminates the distinctive characteristics of each society, traces long-term developments, and offers explanations for these changes. 摘要: 南北對峙的遼、宋、金是中古向近世中國轉變的關鍵時期。本研究全 面收集遼、宋、金出土墓誌，以統計方法分析其使用者，宏觀呈現各朝上層 菁英在「死後世界」的組成與差異。本文發現，各朝墓誌的主要使用者都是官 吏，但整體的使用者身份組成有明顯南、北差異。遼代集中於契丹貴族，北 宋多為地方菁英。南、北差異隨宋金戰爭而擴大。金代隨葬墓誌的上層菁英遽 減，女真貴族亦罕用墓誌。南宋墓誌的隨葬增加，且更集中在官吏與士人， 東南地區亦出現許多新型態的墓誌，推測與理學興起有關。從跨越朝代與 國別的出土墓誌可見南、北社會的特點與發展。

title: Slavery and Zhang Dai’s Aesthetics
abstract: This article argues that the celebrated aesthetics of Tao’an mengyi 陶庵夢憶 by Zhang Dai 張岱 (1597–1689) are inseparable from the system of bonded labor that structured late-imperial Chinese elite culture. Often read as exemplary memory writing, the collection constructs an aesthetic centered on spectacle, surface, and perceptual disorientation. I argue that this aesthetic both depends on and obscures a pervasive system of human commodification, which I approach through the analytic lens of slavery. Drawing on recent scholarship that emphasizes the ubiquity of trafficking, the article shifts focus from defining enslaved populations to examining a broader system of social transactionality. Readings of essays on theater, visual display, and elite sociability show how aesthetic effects rely on the precise coordination—and erasure—of labor. Zhang Dai’s fascination with illusion and perfect staging reflects and reproduces a world structured by mastery over others. At moments, especially in depictions of sex work, this aesthetic distance becomes unstable, revealing underlying tensions. Ultimately, Tao’an mengyi not only represents but enacts an aesthetics of control, inviting readers to participate in transforming domination into aesthetic pleasure. 摘要: 本文主張，張岱之《陶庵夢憶》的美學與晚期帝制中國之依附性勞動體 制密不可分。其審美以奇觀、表面與感知錯置為核心，既奠基於亦遮蔽人身 商品化，本文以「奴隸制」作為分析概念。透過細讀戲曲、展示與社交場景，指 出審美效果依賴對勞動的精密調度並將其抹除，從而再生產支配他人的社 會結構。部分涉及性交易之描寫亦顯露出內在張力。總之，《陶庵夢憶》不 僅再現，亦實踐一種將支配轉化為審美愉悅的控制美學。

title: Learning to Hear: Evidential Scholarship and the Ancient Song in High Qing China
abstract: This article examines the power of song within the High Qing phil-ological movement known as evidential scholarship ( kaozheng xue 考證學). Focusing on the celebrated poet Huang Jingren 黃景仁 (1749–1783) and his association with the influential evidential scholar Zhu Yun 朱筠 (1729–1781) during Zhu’s tenure as education commissioner of Anhui Province, it challenges modern accounts that oppose lyric subjectivity to philological inquiry. I argue that prevailing understandings of both High Qing literature and scholarship fail to apprehend the integral connection between poetic and evidentiary practices in the period. For Qing writers such as Huang and Zhu, the idea of song afforded not merely aesthetic expression but a medium of self-evident, apodictic proof. Close readings of key episodes show how this claim to truth functioned as a nexus of shared immanence wherein writing presents itself as singing and reading unfolds as an act of present listening. By attending to this regime of “notional song,” the study reframes evidential scholarship not as a protoscientific divergence from the poetic but as a culture in which sound, citation, and proof were mutually constitutive. 摘要: 本文探討「歌」在清代盛世考證學語境中的作用。以詩人黃景仁 (1749–1783)及其與朱筠(1729–1781)在安徽學政任內的交往為線索，本 文重新審視近 現代將抒情的內在性對立與考證學術的敘述框架。作者指出，廣為流傳的 對清代文學與學術實踐的論述，往往忽略了詩歌作與考證學之間的內在聯 繫。對黃景仁與朱筠等人而言，「歌」不僅用於審美表達,更發揮著一種自證 自明的媒介作用。本文透過對「歌」的若干關鍵場景的細讀來說明，詩歌的 真理主張是在一種共享的臨在經驗中展開的——書寫在此呈現為歌唱，閱 讀則成為當下的聆聽。從「意念之歌」的角度出發，本文主張考證學不應被 理解為與詩性深具分歧的前科學，而應被納入一種能使聲音、引證與證成彼 此交織、相互生成的文化框架之中。

title: Popular Nanyang: re-thinking Chinese cultures in post-war Singapore and Malaya/Malaysia
abstract: This special issue aims to rethink the significance of “popular culture” for Singapore and Malayan/Malaysian Chinese studies, and more broadly, for modern Chinese cultural studies. Located in the heart of Nanyang, Singapore and Malaya/Malaysia are well-known sites of vibrant Chinese cultural production. After World War Two, besides literature written by intellectuals, cultural forms with wider appeal have enriched the everyday lives of Chinese in the region. From large-scale publishing, to theatre, to radio broadcast, to film and television, the mix of old and new media technologies enlivened by multiple languages and Chinese dialects were entangled with complex commercial and ideological concerns. This special issue frames the resultant sociocultural formation as “Popular Nanyang,” offering a conceptual framework as well that analyse how people’s leisure preferences and ideas about regionality associated with Singapore, Malaya/Malaysia—and beyond—were animated by quotidian and translocal practices of cultural production and consumption. Collectively, the articles demonstrate how the “popular” in its varied senses of extensive reach, non-state positionality, substantial profitability, content accessibility, and contemporary resonance enabled “Nanyang” as a regional imaginary and a cultural sensibility to survive, travel, and reinvent itself across shifting political and historical contexts from the 1950s till the 1990s despite the rise of “Southeast Asia” as the favoured alternative. Advocating for a cultural history of Chinese communities composed from a grassroots perspective, the special issue harnesses the internal diversity of “Popular Nanyang” to point towards a future mode of historical analysis that recognizes the non-Chinese and non-Sinophone dimensions of mass-oriented Nanyang culture.

title: Transborder malleability: examining popular Nanyang through film stardom
abstract: What does it mean to characterise someone, something or somewhere as “Nanyang”? Whether in studies of Nanyang elite or popular cultures, the term is today frequently invoked as a shorthand for a place-based Southeast Asian Chinese identity formed predominantly through acclimatisation to, and interaction with, local cultures and environments, especially in the context of Singapore. This paper rethinks the notion of “popular Nanyang” beyond this usual paradigm through an examination of Singaporean film star Chong Sit Fong’s regional stardom in the 1950s and 1960s. Uncovering how Chong simultaneously embodied different kinds of Chinese national, local and translocal identities, this paper illustrates how the characteristic of transborder malleability, which refers to the capacity to simultaneously embody seemingly contradictory ideologies across borders, enabled Chong to attain regional film stardom during a time of geopolitical flux. This gestures towards an understanding of Nanyang Chineseness not only as place-based, but also inherently translocal and transnational, suggesting how “Nanyang” indexes a flexible modality of identity that functions across geopolitical borders during the 1950s and 1960s.

title: Popular crossings: Lin Chen and his bifurcated editorial practice in 1950s Singapore and Malaya
abstract: This article reframes the Singapore Chinese dramatist Lin Chen’s cultural practice by explicating discrepant modes of popular cultural production and circulation in 1950s Singapore and Malaya through commercial printing. Today, Lin Chen (1919–2004) is remembered primarily as the pioneering playwright-director who shaped Singapore’s Mandarin theatre scene after the second World War. Alongside his amateur theatrical engagements, he served vocationally as an editor at the World Book Company (Shijie Shuju), one of the five major localised Chinese-language publishing houses. It is now revealed that Lin helmed both Linglong (Smart) and Wenyu Shenghuo (Culture and Amusement), two leisure magazines published contemporaneously around the mid-1950s. Whereas Smart carried salacious content, Culture and Amusement promoted “healthy arts and entertainment,” focusing on collective performing art forms. The two publications’ conflicting stances on nurturing readers’ interests placed them on opposing sides of the anti-yellow culture campaign in Singapore, which criticised the widespread societal access to prurient material. Examining the two periodicals in tandem as well as the content within Smart, this article outlines how Lin negotiated fluid ideas about the landscape of mass market publishing that spans the nature of the content, his non-state positionality as a cultural actor, the journals’ audience constituencies, and the contents’ varying degrees of contemporary resonance with the decolonising ethos in Singapore and Malaya. The inter-journal and intra-journal analyses reveal the intransparency of Chinese culture labelled as “yellow” and how the idea of the “popular”—represented through overlapping vernacular senses in Chinese—index an internally dissonant landscape of grassroots culture.

title: Yellow panic: Yao Zi, popular literature and gendered modernity in Cold War Malaya
abstract: During the peak of the anti-yellow cultural movement in Singapore (1953–1956), Yao Zi—now recognised as a pioneering figure in postwar Sinophone Malayan literature—was criticised as a pornographic “yellow” writer. This article explores the cultural debates and phenomena of 1950s Malaya, a period of social transformation in the late colonial era shaped by ideological polarisation during the Cold War and anti-colonial nationalism. It focuses on the moral panic surrounding “yellow”—a term in which concerns surrounding sexuality and Chinese ethnicity intersect—through a historical and cultural analysis of the author Yao Zi’s literary and editorial works. It situates them within broader debates about yellow literature, demonstrating the ways sexuality, ethnicity, and womanhood were constructed as moral categories of social engagement within the Cold War-era battlegrounds of modernity and decolonisation. The first section of this article reexamines the anti-yellow cultural movement and its associated moral discourse by introducing Yao and his conceptualisation of popular literature in Nanyang, showing how they challenged ideological binaries and gender norms during the cultural Cold War. The second section shifts to another dimension of yellow panic: its intersections with Chinese identity and gender. Focusing on the romance genre that secured Yao’s literary prominence, it analyses his lesser-known novella The Storm (1954) for its depiction of women's narrative presence and the Chinese experience of gendered modernity in Malaya, an experience conditioned by a cultural nationalism uneasy with hybridity.

title: Huang Ya’s Wisteria and the Cold War middlebrow: melodrama, Manichean worlds, and Mahua literature
abstract: As the longest-serving editor of the literary magazine Chao Foon, Malaysian Chinese (Mahua) writer Huang Ya (1932–1992) is widely regarded as a central figure in shaping Mahua modernism during the 1960s. Existing scholarship has largely focused on his editorial advocacy for Malayanisation and modern Mahua literature within a Cold War framework, while less attention has been paid to his fiction, which draws more heavily on melodramatic than modernist aesthetics. This article examines Huang’s best-selling romance Wisteria (1960) through the lens of the “Cold War middlebrow,” understood here as a contingent literary formation that served sociocultural, sentimental, and pedagogical functions during a period of polarised ideologies. By analysing Wisteria’s adaptation of the melodramatic mode for a local readership, this article offers a reassessment of what constitutes the “popular” in Mahua literature, showing how Huang’s fiction engaged questions of taste, value, and affect within a rapidly changing decolonising milieu. Through the subversion of melodrama’s Manichean binaries and the reconfiguration of the relationship between modernism and the middlebrow, Huang demonstrates a self-conscious effort to balance accessibility with aesthetic ambition. Situating Wisteria within the intersecting contexts of Cold War cultural politics and inter-Asian literary networks connecting Hong Kong and Malaya, this article highlights how popular Mahua literature participated in the circulation of cultural influences and the forging of new national identities, thereby expanding critical understandings of both “literary value” and the “popular” within the Mahua canon.

title: Reading popular Nanyang: literary realism in plurilingual Singapore
abstract: This article approaches the topic of Nanyang popular culture from the perspective of language use and language politics. Revisiting a canonical text by Miao Xiu, Singapore under the Roofs (1951), which is set in Singapore on the cusp of decolonisation, this article examines the left-leaning realist camp’s engagement with a plurilingual and transnational public sphere where different forms of popular culture—some profit-driven, others politically oriented—competed for resources and audiences. The story’s incorporation of non-Mandarin Chinese languages and non-standard linguistic registers draws attention to how linguistic variations associated with the subaltern class mediate access to their subjectivity. In seeking to broaden the scope of current discussions of the language question beyond the conventional framing of the state’s ideology of language in Singapore, the analysis here refutes the technological determinism inherent in excluding literature in print from popular culture simply because its medium of production has been overtaken by “newer” technologies.

title: Nanyang popular culture on Singapore television (1963–1979)
abstract: This essay explores the film-to-television evolution of the Nanyang popular cultural imaginary between Hong Kong and Singapore in the 1960s and 1970s. Not having the capacity to produce films or television serials, Singapore was heavily reliant on Hong Kong films to fill its airtime, and in so doing, gave the diasporic imaginary projected by films a second lease of life on television. Television was a more capacious medium than film—a wider range of popular cultural performances were featured on its variety shows. The more literary and artistic (wenyi) songs surprisingly sold as well if not better than their liuxing counterparts. Combined, television and popular music remade the Nanyang popular cultural imaginary for Singapore, as the radical left’s Malayanisation cultural vision became increasingly marginalised from the reality of Singapore’s independence and its development in the capitalistic world.

title: Popular Nanyang and the construction of a pluralist Sinophone community: the case of Rediffusion Singapore
abstract: Originating in the UK in 1928 and introduced to Singapore in 1949, the cable radio service Rediffusion gained popularity for its affordable, multi-ethnic programming. In addition to a channel featuring Tamil, Malay, and English content, Rediffusion offered a dedicated Chinese channel that included not only Mandarin programmes but also broadcasts in various Sinitic dialects such as Hokkien, Cantonese, and Teochew. This article examines Rediffusion’s role from the 1950s to the 1970s in fostering a pluralistic Sinophone community in Singapore, collaborating closely with Chinese clan associations organized around Sinitic dialect affiliations. However, this linguistic diversity diminished with the implementation of the “Speak More Mandarin, Less Dialect” policy in 1979. In compliance with the policy, Rediffusion gradually reduced and eventually phased out its dialect programmes. I interpret this shift in Rediffusion’s programming as indicative of Singapore’s increasing linguistic homogenization, despite the People’s Action Party (PAP) government’s efforts to present the nation as multicultural and multilingual. The post-independence rhetoric of fostering a multicultural society with four official languages—English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil—ironically streamlined the diverse Sinophone community into a monolithic one, with Mandarin imposed as the “official” mother tongue for all Sinophone subjects, regardless of their dialect heritage.

title: Projecting “healthy films”: Chong Gay Theatres, youth and Chinese cinema in late Cold War Singapore
abstract: This article examines Chong Gay Theatres’ role in circulating mainland Chinese cinema in Singapore from the 1970s to the 1980s under the leadership of Lim Djit Sun (1925–1987). Known for importing left-leaning Hong Kong films, Chong Gay shifted in the 1980s to Mandarin-language productions from the People’s Republic of China in collaboration with the Shanghai Film Corporation, a transition shaped by the Speak Mandarin Campaign, changing censorship policies, and generational shifts in audience taste. Emerging from networks around the anti-yellow culture movement and earlier left-leaning cultural and entertainment circles, Chong Gay recast progressive cultural ideals through the discourse of “healthy films” within an increasingly regulated media environment. Drawing on archival sources, media reports, and oral interviews, I trace how “healthy films” were redefined through the interaction of ideological commitment and commercial pressure during a period of cultural transition in Singapore. By examining film delegations and festivals in the 1980s, hybrid genres, and youth reception, I argue that Singapore became a key node in late Cold War transregional exchange, where films from Taiwan, Hong Kong, and mainland China converged and were reinterpreted. Intermediaries such as Lim promoted PRC cinema as an edifying alternative to commercial culture while sustaining cultural ties with reform-era China. Singapore thus functioned as a distribution hub and testing ground where PRC films were evaluated and adapted for Southeast Asian audiences. Although officially-sanctioned healthy films were associated with discipline and social harmony, their ambivalent reception reveals unease over the commercialisation of PRC cinema and the persistence of residual leftist sensibilities.

title: Popular culture in the time of Greater Nanyang
abstract: Cognisant of the multivalent, shifting meanings of “Nanyang” as a spatiotemporal, geopolitical, geo-economic, and cultural unit, this article seeks to flesh out the concept of “Popular Nanyang” by bringing in the contributions of popular culture from the Philippines, Indonesia, and Thailand. Historically, ethnic Chinese played an important role in the creation of “the popular,” albeit often dismissed as commercial or of low cultural value, in the plurilingual settings of their respective domiciles. Their networked production, distribution, circulation, consumption, and (e)valuation of popular culture helped substantiate the reach and bounds of “Nanyang” as geography, market, and regional imaginary. This article reclaims and repurposes the term “Greater Nanyang” to give weight to Southeast Asia, Hong Kong, Taiwan, and Macao as hubs for the multi-sited co-creation of the Popular Nanyang from the Cold War era to the end of the twentieth century. The Greater Nanyang concept highlights the historicity, materiality, politics, economies, ecologies, and cultures of localisation, meaning-making, and value creation that underpin place-, identity-, and claim-making in, across, and beyond the region. The temporal depth of Popular Nanyang also raises questions about Sinophone assumptions of the convergence of language, audience, cultural literacy, and ethnicity in the production, circulation, and consumption of popular culture.

title: Mobility, variety, and community in popular Nanyang entertainment from the 1930s to the 1970s

title: Perverted normalcy: on the cultural durability of authoritarianism
abstract: Authoritarianism in Indonesia persists not only through institutions and coercion, but through everyday understandings of what constitutes normal life. This article develops the concept of perverted normalcy to explain that persistence. Following a historical trajectory from Dutch colonialism through the New Order to the post-Reformasi present, it argues that unresolved violence has accumulated within social relations, shaping expectations, habits, and the limits of political imagination. Violence does not simply leave wounds in the past. It helps establish the terms on which the present is lived. The article examines how this condition took shape, survived democratic transition, and found renewed expression through digital governance. It then traces its reproduction across generations through family, education, media, and silence. These are the everyday settings in which domination becomes familiar, and its historical origins disappear from view. Perverted normalcy thus directs attention to a problem that institutional reform alone cannot resolve. Understanding authoritarian persistence across the region requires examining how histories of violence become ordinary social life, and how democratic transformation might interrupt their reproduction within the relationships and practices that organize everyday existence.

title: “Asia” in the making: friction, relational authorship, and the pedagogy of productive discomfort in the Asia Documentary Co-Production Network: A critical autoethnography of transnational Zoom workshops, 2021–2026
abstract: This article argues that “Asia,” as a category of regional belonging, is not a precondition of transnational collaboration but a relation produced within it—assembled, incrementally and unevenly, in the friction of cross-border documentary co-production. Drawing on the Asia Documentary Co-Production Network (ADCN), a hybrid pedagogical project linking film schools across East and Southeast Asia, it reads the transcripts of monthly online meetings, rather than the finished films, as its primary text. Through a critical autoethnography written from the position of a faculty mentor and former chair, it traces friction in two directions: outward, where students raised in mutual national hostility come to reference one another laterally and so constitute the region in real time; and inward, where an encounter with another nation’s history estranges students from their own. Building a single conceptual chain from Tsing’s friction through platform mediation and radical listening to Chen’s inter-Asian referencing and critical syncretism, the article shows these concepts being enacted at the smallest scale—by undergraduates, over poor connections—and, crucially, where they fail. Against celebratory accounts of frictionless online collaboration, it insists on asymmetry: of resource, of language, and of the mentor’s power to redirect. “Asia” so understood is closer to a verb than a noun—permanently unfinished, and real in the measure of that unfinishedness.

title: Epistemological friction in the contact zone: Ethiopian itinerant commerce, socio-cultural articulation, and the unlearning of race in Chinese trade cities
abstract: This article introduces the concept of racial unlearning to examine how racism is deconstructed within micro-level Afro-Chinese interactions. Drawing on longitudinal data generated among Ethiopian traders who travel between Ethiopia and China, I situate Ethio-Chinese encounters within Bhabha’s [Bhabha, Homi K. [1994] 2004. The Location of Culture. London: Routledge] “in-between spaces”—interstitial zones of fractured hegemony in which African agency produces not merely epistemic articulation but ontological consequence, carving out deracialised social realities. In these spaces, blackness and Chineseness emerge as liminal identities that evolve towards mutual recognition through iterative processes of racial unlearning. I argue that, within localised Afro-Chinese interactions, racialisation and racial unlearning unfold as concomitant processes—a dynamic that dominant global racial discourses have failed to anticipate. This reorientation shifts analytical attention away from macro- and meso-level scholarship preoccupied with the formation of racial hierarchies, and towards blackness and Chineseness as active, lived, and relationally constituted experiences.

title: Why Do We Need Taiwan Studies in the Twenty-First Century?
abstract: This article reviews scholarly literature related to Taiwan from the 1950s to the present to depict the development of Taiwan studies, its fraught relationship with China studies, and Taiwan scholars’ search for a home of their own. I explore the expansion in research focus from anthropology in the 1950s and 1960s, to political science in the 1970s, to economics in the 1980s, and to literary and culture studies in the 1990s and describe how scholars established associations, research centres, programmes, and a journal devoted to Taiwan studies. This institutionalisation has created a feeling among scholars of being ‘at home’ and led me to the question of which routes should be taken for the future development of the field: the ‘ Sinocentric ’ (strikethrough intentional) route of working with China studies, or the alternative, ‘oceanic’ route of seeking alliances with other marginalised countries that also believe in freedom, democracy, and resistance to hegemony.

title: Going Weigen: Animal Advocacy and Sustainability Intersections under Taiwan’s New Vegan Movement
abstract: From compassion to animal liberation, health, and sustainability, veganism is a concept in flux in Taiwan as a new generation of actors are bringing a fresh face and tactics to a novel yet familiar practice. This article examines the emergence of Taiwan’s new vegan movement during the socially receptive period that followed the Sunflower Movement. It introduces the actors involved in vegan advocacy, noting its distinct routes of diffusion, and where new vegan identities and alternative advocacy spaces play a key role. It shows that while animal rights rationales informed the inception of the contemporary vegan movement, some actors have shifted their attention to policy processes by reconnecting their discourses to matters of dietary sustainability, thus bringing the local movement into closer alignment with global vegan mainstreaming through engagement with sustainability regimes.

title: Save the Children: Youth Narratives and Historical Learning in Three Taiwanese Horror Video Games
abstract: This article examines the process of historical learning in video gaming and broadens the scope of Taiwanese game culture through an in-depth analysis of three horror video games: Detention (2017), pagui (2019), and Halflight (2020). It offers a comparative study of these games, focusing on their shared ‘save the children’ theme, which reimagines Taiwan’s traumatic past through nightmarish settings tied to the February 28 Incident and the White Terror. Additionally, the article explores how youth narratives shape and mobilise players through interactive digital gameplay. By blending historical memory with horror aesthetics, these meticulously crafted games serve as immersive portals, allowing players to engage with Taiwan’s past in a deeply interactive and affective manner.

title: Entanglement in an Endangered Situation: Paiwan Society and the Conservation of the Mountain Hawk-Eagle
abstract: The mountain hawk-eagle has a special status among the indigenous Paiwan people of Taiwan. This article examines the historical evolution of the use of this eagle’s feathers amid social transformations within Paiwan culture. It also addresses the bird’s endangered status and proposed conservation strategies to protect it. Wildlife management collaborations between indigenous communities and conservationists have sparked conflicts in values and worldviews that are challenging to reconcile. While the Paiwan wish to continue using the eagle’s feathers in important cultural rituals, this increased demand exacerbates hunting pressures on the species. This article seeks to find a better balance between preserving cultural practices and ensuring species survival. Drawing on four years of fieldwork among the Paiwan, it demonstrates the complexities of navigating entangled human–animal relationships in the context of species endangerment.

title: Contextualising Fragments Containing Fresh Perspectives about the Spanish Settlements in Taiwan (1636–1638)
abstract: This article examines extracts relating to the period 1636–1638 in Taiwan, when the Spanish occupied two settlements in northern Taiwan, one of them being abandoned in 1637. These fragments reveal fresh perspectives on Taiwan as a stepping stone between the Philippines, the Ryukyu islands, and mainland China, giving rare first-hand accounts of the perils of journeys to these places from Taiwan’s Spanish settlements in the 1630s. The extracts also reveal fresh aspects to Spanish relationships with Taiwan’s Indigenous people. These descriptions add to arguments that the Indigenous people had a significant influence on the departure of the Spanish from the island. The fragmentary details in these texts give further evidence of the multinational exchange that took place during those years. To analyse these fragments, a thematic analysis places them at the centre of discussions, to explore what they add to existing knowledge about the settlements during those years.

title: Revelations from the Taiwanese Netflix Series Wave Makers: #MeToo, Sexual Violence, and the Lesbian Continuum
abstract: This article discusses critical issues explored in the Taiwanese ‘Netflix Originals’ series, Wave Makers (dir. Lin Chun-yang, 2023) and highlights their real-life implications in Taiwan and other societies of Chinese heritage. The fact that the series has triggered Taiwan’s belated #MeToo movement showcases the profound impact it has had on Taiwanese audiences, especially regarding conventional narratives surrounding power-based sexual violence, gender inequalities at the workplace, and attitudes towards homosexuality. Using both narrative and discourse analyses, this article unpacks such narratives by providing theoretical readings – both feminist and constructionist – for the series’ various plots and character transformations. Divulged in this process are the hidden social and ideological mechanisms within the Taiwanese context that have perpetuated gender inequalities at the workplace and in the family.

title: Taiwan and China: Whither to Go?, written by Hsiu-Lien Lu

From Development to Democracy: The Transformation of Modern Asia, written by Dan Slater and Joseph Wong
