Sinophone Studies Across Disciplines: A Reader, written by Howard Chiang and Shu-mei Shih
Crisis Communication in a Public Health Emergency: Examining Taiwan and Singapore Government Press Releases through Latent Topic Modelling
authors: Raphael Duerr; Honeylet Santos; Yvan Ysmael Yonaha
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic was an unprecedented public health emergency requiring concerted government action. Government responsibilities included communicating risks, informing the public about hygiene practices, and combating disinformation. Examining government communication strategies is important for improving crisis communication in future emergencies. Using quantitative text analyses, this article examines approximately 3,000 press releases issued by the Taiwanese and Singaporean governments. Topic prevalence was examined in relation to the timing of press releases and COVID-19 case and death counts. We find that both governments employed high-frequency, highly standardised, and detail-rich communication. Their communication strategies correspond closely with the model proposed by the Crisis and Emergency Risk Communication (CERC) framework, with their focus shifting from the initial shock of the pandemic through to the resolution stage, when vaccines were deployed. Their communication demonstrated a commitment to being first, being right, and being credible, while their guidelines promoted action by providing the public with concrete measures to reduce risk. Nevertheless, empathy was not prominent in the press releases, which may reflect both the limitations of the format and a division of communicative roles between bureaucratic and executive institutions.

title: Taiwan and the Global Cold War: Histories, Legacies, and New Directions
authors: James Lin; Bi-yu Chang; Evan Dawley; Mei-fen Kuo; Chih-Ming Wang; Dominic Meng-Hsuan Yang

Performing ‘Two Sides, One Family’ in the Cloud: Cross-Strait Popular Religious Exchanges During the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: This article investigates the adaptations made across the Taiwan Strait to sustain popular religious exchanges during the COVID-19 pandemic. Drawing on observations of cross-Strait virtual events and in-depth interviews, it examines the major exchange formats that emerged during this period and assesses their broader implications. The findings reveal that the materiality of divine efficacy in popular religions rendered pilgrimage activities impossible, while formats driven by the ‘United Front’ strategy of the Chinese Communist Party proved more resilient. Previously institutionalised exchange platforms migrated online, and virtual settings facilitated new connections. However, these virtual events also brought unscripted and diverse Taiwanese expressions into direct view, unsettling the carefully choreographed narrative of cross-Strait unity that had previously structured these exchanges. The immediate post-pandemic recovery has been primarily facilitated by the party-state’s United Front objectives. While the pandemic disruptions were temporary, they have ultimately reinforced the political and economic foundations upon which cross-Strait religious networks now rest.

title: Seeking the koko’ ta’ay: Investigating the Origins of Little People Myths in Taiwan and Beyond, edited by Tobie Openshaw and Dean Karalekas
Uneasy Encounters: Christian Churches in Greater China, written by Magdaléna Rychetská
Rebirth as Redemptive Spectrality: Hauntological Narratives in Li Ang’s Paranormal Trilogy
abstract: Li Ang’s paranormal trilogy— Visible Ghosts , Possession , and The River Woman Beyond —employs ghostly narratives to stage the intersection of historical trauma, gendered violence, and ethical reckoning. Drawing on Jacques Derrida’s hauntology and Judith Butler’s theory of grievability, this article argues that the ghost in Li Ang’s fiction functions not merely as a motif but as a structural condition of perception and narration. Across the trilogy, spectrality becomes the medium through which histories are re-entered, not to restore coherence but to expose absence, injury, and unresolved memory. Li Ang does not simply represent the paranormal; she inhabits it. Through increasingly self-referential writing, she stages haunting as a feminist modality of critique and redemption. The paranormal, in this context, is neither superstition nor metaphor—it is the very terrain through which the unspeakable is rendered thinkable, and the unreadable, legible.

title: Consuming Democracy: Geopolitics, Human Rights, and Tourism in Taiwan
abstract: International tourism has been an area where Taiwan has projected its soft power. Tourism involves constructing an identity for the outside world to see, and tourism as ‘placemaking’ requires the deliberate selection of imagery and rhetoric that will represent and synopsise the history, culture, and environment of a location. This article examines democracy and human rights in Taiwan’s tourism landscape and argues that Taiwan’s experience of political transformation is becoming a vital component of its tourism identity under the Democratic Progressive Party government. Emphasising Taiwan’s democratic achievements helps it to build a collective memory of its democratic citizenry, distinguish itself from the People’s Republic of China, and garner support among Western liberal democracies. At the same time, it may reduce the complexity of Taiwan’s political transformations by integrating them into a linear narrative of success and closure.

title: BCOF at eighty: new perspectives on the British commonwealth occupation force in the occupation of Japan
abstract: The British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) component of the Allied Occupation of Japan (1945-1952) has often been overlooked by researchers because of its minimal role in policy-making. Taking the opportunity of the 80th anniversary of the arrival of the first BCOF personnel in Japan, this special issue introduces new perspectives about the organisation based on a range of hitherto unused or under-utilised sources. The introduction begins by emphasising how BCOF’s commanding officer sought to draw attention to his troops’ contribution to the Occupation. There follows a brief overview of the existing secondary research about BCOF in English and in Japanese. The latter half of the introduction outlines the contribution that the four articles make to the special issue. Taken as a whole, the purpose of the special issue is to begin to reassess how the occupiers and the occupied understood the role and meaning of BCOF. The introduction concludes with a call for other researchers to take part in the process of making this reassessment.

title: Japan’s ‘multiple occupations’: ceremonial parades, ritual practices, and the performance of authority in the BCOF
abstract: The Allied occupation of Japan is most commonly remembered through the dominant image of General Douglas MacArthur and a largely American-led occupation regime. Such representations, reinforced by political authority, the concentration of media institutions in Tokyo, and post-war commemorative practices, have long framed the occupation as a singular and coherent project. This article challenges that narrative by advancing the concept of ‘multiple occupations’ to capture the uneven, regionally differentiated realities of occupation governance in post-war Japan. Rather than treating regional diversity as a secondary effect of a unified occupation, the concept foregrounds how authority itself was constituted through differentiated practices across space. Focusing on the early activities of the BCOF (British Commonwealth Occupation Force), a multinational and multi-ethnic force operating primarily in the Chūgoku and Shikoku regions between mid-1946 and mid-1948, the article examines how occupation authority was performed, negotiated, and sustained beyond Tokyo. Although formally subordinate to GHQ/SCAP (General Headquarters/Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers), the BCOF exercised a degree of practical autonomy in day-to-day regional administration while facing internal tensions rooted in imperial hierarchies, racialised divisions, and declining morale. The article further argues that ceremonial practices – notably military parades, musical performances, and funeral processions – played a central role in managing these challenges. Rather than treating such rituals as peripheral or purely symbolic, this article conceptualises them as practical mechanisms of governance. These ceremonies functioned simultaneously as outward-facing performances that communicated legitimacy to Japanese audiences and as inward-facing practices that disciplined personnel and reinforced cohesion within a fragmented occupying force. Drawing on military newspapers, Japanese local and national press, and archival photographs, the study foregrounds the regional experience of occupation and the cultural performance of authority in public space. By recovering the overlooked role of the BCOF and situating it within a framework of multiple occupations, this article complicates dominant narratives of post-war Japan and contributes to broader debates on power, representation, and transnational encounter in modern Japanese history.

title: British veteran reflections on the British Commonwealth Occupation Force and experiences in Japan during the Korean War
abstract: British Commonwealth participation in the Allied Occupation of Japan is a largely overlooked episode in post-war history. Yet at peak, the British Commonwealth Occupation Forces (BCOF) stationed in Japan numbered a sizeable 37,000 personnel from Australia, India, New Zealand and Britain, spread across the Chūgoku and Shikoku regions, including Hiroshima and the key naval port of Kure. BCOF’s missions were to pursue the demilitarisation and demobilisation of Japan, and to promote democratisation, but historians have tended to downplay BCOF’s achievements or overlook it entirely. This paper reassesses BCOF by considering its afterlife during the Korean War, as the British Commonwealth Forces Korea (BCFK) overlapped with BCOF and continued to use its facilities beyond BCOF’s disbanding in 1952. Examining approximately 800 reflections of former British BCOF/BCFK service personnel collected in the 1990s and early 2000s, this paper argues that for many former personnel the experience in Japan helped them to reconcile with Britain’s former wartime enemy (Japan) through personal interactions with Japanese people that generated mutual respect and lasting friendships. In this way BCOF was, for British veterans, an important part of facilitating an improvement in Anglo-Japanese relations at a grassroots level.

title: Occupied Japan through British eyes: recollections of the veterans of the British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) and the British Commonwealth Forces Korea (BCFK)
abstract: This study examines the perceptions by veterans who served in the British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) and the British Commonwealth Forces Korea (BCFK) of the Japanese during their post-war deployment in Japan. Drawing on the recollections of 819 veterans, it explores how such perceptions were shaped by their experiences—ranging from encounters with the devastation of Hiroshima and interactions with local communities to lingering memories of wartime atrocities. While resentment arising from the mistreatment of prisoners of war frequently influenced their attitudes, interactions with Japanese civilians fostered a more nuanced understanding. A comparative analysis with British veterans’ own experiences of the Blitz further contextualizes their views, offering insight into their evolving perspectives. This study also traces a shift in perception—from witnessing the destruction of Hiroshima as an emblem of wartime devastation to recognizing it as a site of historical reflection and learning. Ultimately, it argues that those recollections, despite their fragmentary and sometimes contradictory nature, provide valuable insights into post-war reconciliation and the complexities of cross-cultural relationships.

title: Writing BCOF as diary, re-writing the occupation as memoir
abstract: This article examines the diaries and memoir written by an Australian soldier who fought in the Second World War (1939-1945) and who served in the British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) in the Occupation of Japan. The diaries from 1938 to 1945 contextualise how the soldier wrote about BCOF as an important time in his military career. His BCOF diaries (1946-1951) indicate that he was torn between pursuing relationships with local women and trying to secure promotion. This tension lessened towards the end of his BCOF service but never entirely disappeared. In his memoir written in the mid-1960s he re-wrote his experience in BCOF so that the organisation had a greater moral coherence. These writings by the same individual therefore reveal the process by which a good occupation narrative was formed by rewriting, omission and substitution from the personal memory of the diary to the intended public memory of the memoir.

title: Political allegories of WWII in Haruki Murakami’s works: Johnnie Walker, Colonel Sanders, and the commendatore
abstract: This paper explores the political allegories embedded in Kafka on the Shore (2002) (Murakami Citation2005), arguing that the novel functions as a historical allegory of World War II, urging contemporary Japanese society to confront its wartime responsibilities. While Haruki Murakami’s works have often been perceived as politically disengaged, this study demonstrates how Kafka on the Shore contains hidden political metaphors referencing both Nazi Germany and the Japanese Empire. Employing close reading and historical contextual analysis, this paper examines key figures—Johnnie Walker, Colonel Sanders, and the imagery of the painting ‘Kafka on the Shore’—to reveal how Murakami engages with historical memory. The conflict between Johnnie Walker and Nakata is interpreted as an allegory of British-Japanese imperial rivalry, while Colonel Sanders symbolizes the Americanization of postwar Japan. Moreover, recurring German references, including a Volkswagen car and the ‘Edelweiss’ song from The Sound of Music (Citation1965), serve as reminders of Japan’s wartime alliance with Germany. The study further suggests that Murakami’s later novel, Killing Commendatore (2017) (Murakami Citation2018), adopts a more explicit approach to political allegory, shifting interpretive agency from the reader to the protagonist. By uncovering these layered political metaphors, this paper highlights Murakami’s evolving engagement with historical responsibility in his fiction.

title: Disaster Journalism in Post-3.11 Japan – The Commitment of Yoshida Chia, Free Writer
abstract: The free writer Yoshida Chia represents an example of the engagement of disaster journalism after the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear accident in 2011. Since the Tōhoku triple disaster, Yoshida has devoted her career to reporting information from the refugee shelters provided for people from the evacuated zones of the Fukushima Prefecture. At the core of her journalistic inquiries lie evacuation and post-evacuation issues. By directly interviewing the refugees – especially mothers and children – Yoshida has provided access to information concerning life at the refugee shelters, underlining the political and economic burdens as well as the psychological and social costs that the post-3.11 disaster (in)justice provoked on the affected communities. After introducing the state of art in disaster journalism in Japan with particular emphasis on the role of women journalists in the media, this study examines the new professional figure of the ‘free writer’ presenting the case of Yoshida Chia and her commitment to aiding public engagement in coping with disaster (in)justice during the process of Tōhoku’s recovery. In order to do so, the focus of this article will be on Yoshida’s Reportage of the evacuation of mothers and children. The nuclear victims will fade (2016) and After Fukushima. People who live after the nuclear accident (2018).

title: The First World War and Japan’s cabinet system: how the conflict changed the perception and reception of foreign constitutional models by Japanese elites (1912–1920)
abstract: The modern Japanese state, built on the Meiji Constitution (1889–1947), has long been understood as inspired by a Prussian model. Recent historiography, however, emphasises a paradigm shift in Japanese national identity after the First World War and the development of party politics in the 1920s. How did the experience of this conflict alter the vision of European constitutional frameworks and the choice of foreign models for interpreting Japan’s own political institutions? This article, while focusing on the cabinet system, addresses this question by analysing constitutional commentaries and reform projects by scholars, statesmen, and journalists across three chronological stages. First, it shows that doctrinal debates from 1912 to 1914 were polarised by ideologies favouring the German or British models. Second, it observes essential changes in information pipelines during the war, a detachment from Germany, and increasing praise for Britain’s resilience. Third, it argues that reform projects by influential actors in the war’s immediate aftermath were designed after the United Kingdom’s recent institutional evolutions. These considerations shed light on an early stage of the global dissemination of the Westminster model and suggest its influence went beyond the Dominions and the post-Second World War Commonwealth.

title: Ambiguously queer: interrogating youth and queerness in Kyoto Animation’s adaptation of Sound! Euphonium
abstract: Found across a wide variety of genres, youth is a popular setting for media in Japan. Often focused on school club activities, narratives set during adolescence feature intense relationships between members of the same sex that toe the line between homoromantic and homosocial. The language used in the texts and by the creators often supports both readings, with the audience left to draw their own conclusions based on how they understand youth. While previous scholarship has looked at queerness in youth-focused texts, less has been written about how the association a text has with youth affects queer readings of the language of the texts. Through a textual and discourse analysis of the anime Sound! Euphonium (2015–2024), as well as published interviews with creators and online fan discussion about it, this article interrogates the relationship between queerness and youth in the Japanese media. I argue that youth has a normative effect in the Japanese media sphere, obfuscating the existence of queer readings by providing a normative explanation for even the queerest of language. I further suggest that Sound! Euphonium more widely reflects the ambiguity that pervades representations of queerness during female adolescence in the Japanese media.

title: Ministerial Power in Kantei-Led Policymaking: The Case of the Priority Reform Promotion System for National Universities under the Second Abe Administration
abstract: This article examines the policymaking process of the Priority Reform Promotion System, a performance-based funding system for Japanese national universities introduced under the second Abe administration. Existing research has largely portrayed this process through the lens of Kantei-led (prime minister’s office-led) policymaking, which sees the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) as following directives set by prime ministerial councils. However, little attention has been paid to whether and how MEXT’s own preferences were incorporated into the policy design. Using policy documents and elite interviews with MEXT civil servants, this article traces the policymaking process from agenda setting to the final budget negotiations, taking seriously the agency of MEXT. The findings show that MEXT held clear preferences from an early stage and shaped the design of the system within the new Kantei-led structure. These findings indicate that the Kantei-led framework does not on its own explain who determines specific policy content and suggest that ministerial agency deserves closer attention in analyses of Japan’s centralised policymaking structure.

title: Forging a Double Diaspora: Cuban Jewish Migration and Settlement in 1960s Greater Miami
abstract: After the 1959 revolution, Jewish migrants joined the waves of emigrants exiting Fidel Castro's Cuba. They developed a close-knit community in Greater Miami as their parents and grandparents had done when they immigrated to Cuba decades earlier. Analyzing oral histories, newspapers, and Cuban and US community records, this article uncovers an often-untold history and reconceptualizes diaspora by exploring the local influences on Cuban Jewish diaspora formation for a population belonging to multiple racialized groups. In the decades after arrival in Greater Miami, Cuban Jews transitioned from Cuban nationals to Cuban exiles to US residents and citizens. They found affordable housing in the white-designated Miami Beach and carved out an enclave, connecting Cuban Jewish newcomers and grounding them in the city. To integrate, the migrants felt they had to prove their worth to the larger society, and they embraced respectability politics to defuse their perceived otherness—which contained a complex combination of racial, ethnic, and religious elements—while maintaining their Cuban identity. Cuban Jews forged a double diaspora rooted in an entangled Cuban Jewish identity born from Jewish life in Cuba, cultural adaptation to the US socio-political environment, and interactions with other Cuban exiles and Miami residents.

title: Little Guyana in Motion: Belonging, Religion, and Moral Community in Post–1965 Immigrant New York
abstract: This article argues that post-1965 immigrant New York is often analyzed through two largely parallel literatures—migration and community formation, on the one hand, and religion and transnational devotion, on the other—and that reading them together clarifies how belonging in the outer boroughs was made through overlapping material and moral infrastructures. Bringing the urban scholarship of Nancy Foner, Steven Gregory, Madhulika Khandelwal, and Pyong Gap Min into conversation with work on immigrant religion by R. Stephen Warner, Peggy Levitt, Prema Kurien, and R. Scott Hanson, it demonstrates that labor markets, housing corridors, and neighborhood politics frequently intertwined with ritual calendars, congregational institution-building, and everyday ethics of obligation and care. This article, then, uses the relative absence of the Indo-Guyanese community of Richmond Hill, Queens (“Little Guyana”) from both literatures to probe the limits of frameworks that privilege either “settlement” or “transnationalism.” Drawing on Queens-based community and ethnic press coverage of Phagwah/Holi and Diwali, municipal recognitions such as permits, proclamations, and street co-namings, documentation of mandir-building and temple openings, and oral histories with mandir participants and organizers, it traces devotional circulation between Queens and Guyana as a form of neighborhood-making. This Richmond Hill case shows how ritual processions, institutional expansion, and public commemoration make belonging legible through urban space while sustaining obligations and attachments across borders—treating the neighborhood less as an end point of migration than as a node in a wider devotional circuit.

title: Collective Care Is Essential: Puerto Rican Feminist Activists and Welfare Rights Organizing after 1960
abstract: In 1970, a Puerto Rican woman named Juanita Serrano was elected to serve as a chair of the National Welfare Rights Organization (NWRO) after spending numerous years organizing poor women in Cleveland, Ohio. In this role Serrano joined welfare rights organizers from across the country as they protested the social, economic, and political conditions faced by poor people. This article provides a history of Puerto Rican women's contributions to welfare rights organizing in the United States. It argues that Puerto Rican women activists within the welfare rights movement articulated a vision of collective care that insisted that working-class people should have control over social welfare institutions and that welfare recipients should dictate the forms that care took in their communities. Their vision also addressed Puerto Ricans’ experience as colonial citizens, migrants, Spanish speakers, and people of color. The article examines how demands for collective care were advanced both in organizing to improve social welfare programs in the United States and Puerto Rico, and in leftist political mobilizations that contested capitalism and colonialism. Thus, one of the particularities of Puerto Rican welfare rights activism was that it was often closely linked to broader struggles for colonial migrants’ rights and for the decolonization of Puerto Rico.

title: Immigration, Authoritarian Populism, and Donald Trump
abstract: Donald Trump fueled a political rise by exploiting the issue of immigration. Rejecting the liberal narrative of a “nation of immigrants” that had long portrayed the United States as a land of opportunity for all and a haven for the oppressed, Trump turned the idea of immigration into an existential threat to the nation itself. He dehumanized people crossing American borders with wild abandon, calling them criminals, drug dealers, “dog-eaters,” invaders, rapists, pollutants of the nation's blood supply, and monsters capable of entering the kitchens of citizens to “slit their throat.” In his first run for the presidency in 2016, he promised to build a massive wall on the southern border. In his second inaugural address, in 2025, he declared a national emergency at the border and said he would send military forces to “repel a disastrous invasion.” Why did Trump do this? Why did he turn immigrants—both undocumented and legal—into extreme threats to the nation? Was he simply a radical xenophobe or racist seeking to keep America mostly white or Anglo-Saxon? And where did this extreme form of hostility come from? This essay seeks to probe these issues and offers an interpretation of matters that will be debated for years to come. It argues that in his rhetoric and deeds, Trump's immigration policies need to be understood as more than a resort to traditional forms of American xenophobia and racism. His narrative of immigration as a peril was a means to a larger end that sought to overturn liberal democracy in the United States with a form of authoritarianism.

Becoming Chinese American: The Chin Siblings During China’s War of Resistance
abstract: The Chin siblings, three second-generation Chinese Americans, went to their ancestral land to teach at institutions of higher education during China’s War of Resistance against Japanese Invasion (1931–1945). While there, they availed themselves of opportunities that were denied to Chinese Americans in the U.S. but also faced prejudice and suspicion. Nonetheless, in family and business correspondence they often portrayed themselves as patriotic citizens of both countries and cultural ambassadors who connected the two peoples. They employed such efforts to negotiate competing nationalist demands made by the Chinese and U.S. governments and thus offered invaluable insights into the complex processes of becoming Chinese American. This article shines a light on a significant yet little known body of materials to demonstrate how family dynamics, as well as political, racial, and cultural forces, shaped the identify formation of Chinese Americans in the mid-twentieth century, especially immediately preceding, during, and after World War II. Ultimately, it builds up the archives of Asian American history and amplifies Asian American voices from the unique perspective of a sibling unit’s wartime experiences.

title: Making the AAPI Perspectives Oral History Project: Remembering a Place-Based Social History of Activism in Santa Clara Valley
abstract: This article examines the AAPI Perspectives: Oral History and Activism Digital Archive and Curriculum Project (2021–2024), which redirected county funding from carceral “hate crime” initiatives to community-based oral history. The article proceeds in three parts: first, it contextualizes the project’s genesis in the early 2020s; second, it analyzes the project’s oral history interviews to show how these AAPI social histories took actual place in Santa Clara Valley (1840s–present); and third, it argues that these overlapping regional histories facilitated an intergenerational, multiethnic spatial politics that catalyzed various activisms, which seeded social movements, advanced Asian American studies, and challenged the model minority myth. Together, these analyses highlight the potential of grassroots organizing and oral history to generate community-centered narratives that echo the founding vision of Asian American studies as a field committed to “serving the people.” AAPI Perspectives reframes AAPI pasts while modeling how communities can reclaim, preserve, and mobilize their histories in the pursuit of justice.

title: (De)Tracking Sinocentrism: Mathematics Education + Racialized Electoral Politics in San Francisco
authors: Kyle L. Chong (張陳創庭); Sheila M. Orr
abstract: In 2024, San Francisco voters approved Proposition G, requiring 8th-grade Algebra 1 for public school students and restores “tracked” course sequences that sort students by their perceived intellectual abilities. Proposition G’s proponents mobilized anti-Asian American racist essentialism, and proximity to whiteness, targeting San Francisco’s large Chinese American electorate. We argue, using Asian Critical Race Theory and critical race discourse analysis, that Proposition G proponents’ arguments mobilized covert anti-Asian American essentialism and Sinocentrism to undermine racial justice discourses in educational politics. We consequently propose an analytic of “(De) Tracking Sinocentrism,” which disentangles Sinocentrism from Asian American panethnic racialization processes.

Introduction
abstract: Before the Unicode Standard, text shared across digital devices was often garbled, a problem that disproportionately affected users of non-Latin scripts. Unicode's emergence in the 1990s resolved this by encoding the world's major scripts into a single global standard that made text interoperable across digital devices—a development especially consequential in Asia, home to more than 90 percent of non-Latin script users. Yet Unicode is not a neutral infrastructure. Each encoding decision—which characters to include, how to handle script boundaries, whether to unify Sinographs across linguistic traditions—was shaped by the competing interests of large technology companies, national governments, user communities, and scholars. And each carried enduring political implications. This introduction argues that it is time for humanities scholars to critically engage with the ways in which Unicode crystallized at the intersection of state power, capital, and culture to become the foundation of a global infrastructure that governs nearly all textual communication today. It situates the four articles in this volume within the existing scholarly literature, provides a glossary of key technical terms, and introduces the closing roundtable in which technical experts and humanities scholars reflect on the field's future directions.

title: Big Tech, the Big State, and the Battle for Encoding All of the World's Languages
abstract: For over three decades, the dominant narrative of Unicode has been that it is a technical solution to a technical problem of global communication. This article argues that this narrative has dominated the discourse about Unicode because it is the narrative of the victors. Understanding the social and political interests at stake requires returning to the battle that yielded the Unicode Standard as the sole universal encoding standard: a period from 1988, when a draft proposal of the Unicode Standard was first made public, to 1993, when the Unicode Standard effectively conquered the dominant encoding standard, ISO/IEC 10646. Whereas Unicode was an organization consisting mostly of engineers at large American software companies, ISO was an international standard organization comprising representatives from member nations. Their confrontation over the encoding of Sinographs pitted big tech against the big state, with significant national and financial interests at stake. The last section discusses how a recent attempt by the Chinese state to rapidly encode a large batch of Sinographs used in proper names reveals some of the stakes of this ongoing negotiation between big tech and big states.

title: ISCII Imperialism
abstract: In 2009, Daniel Pargman and Jacob Palme published an essay titled “ASCII Imperialism,” which discussed how the American text standard, ASCII, was embedded in existing computer protocols and how it marginalized non-English languages. This article hearkens to that concept by calling for the recognition of “ISCII imperialism.” It examines how the little-known Indian Script Code for Information Interchange (ISCII) has been integrated in global communication protocols since 1991 through the Unicode Standard and has created the potential for an uneven digital landscape for different Indian languages and writing systems. Specifically, ISCII has been controversial for seemingly privileging Devanagari, commonly used to write Hindi, at the expense of other scripts. Public outcry against ISCII imperialism has been transformative, however. As this article demonstrates, advocacy by Indic script communities has pushed the Unicode Consortium to reconsider its implementation of ISCII, demonstrating how even rigid technical structures are influenced by regional language politics.

title: Abstract Code
abstract: Unicode is everywhere and nowhere at once. Since its invention in 1993 by lucrative American companies, including Xerox, Apple, and Microsoft, Unicode has been the global standard for information exchange, enabling the transfer of data across the world by converting more than a hundred and sixty world scripts into standardized bits and bytes. Its spread throughout the world is so expansive, its technical complexity so elaborate, and its integration into daily lives so seamless that Unicode has become a natural part of the world—used everywhere, yet seen nowhere. This article seeks to denaturalize Unicode by examining its origins from a global perspective and situating it within a longer history of script engineering that was deeply intertwined with imperialism, colonialism, and capitalism. It proposes the term “abstract code” to capture a historical process whereby capitalism homogenizes and standardizes diverse cultures of writing to make them exchangeable and commensurable with one another in the market of information. Disclosing the historical links between the nineteenth-century age of script engineering and the birth of Unicode in the 1980s, this article demonstrates that the new information infrastructure sought to abstract all writing systems into a standardized sequence of bits and thus enable the corporate accumulation of capital at a global scale. Unicode, in short, was the critical infrastructure that enabled the birth of a global neoliberal information economy.

title: Literary Expression at the Ends of Unicode
abstract: This article examines how Unicode reshapes the humanities by asking what happens when a supposedly universal encoding system meets the demands of the Japanese writing system. Focusing on EnJoe Toh's 2018 collection A Whirlpool of Glyphs, it shows how his fiction probes the tension between standardization and expression that underlies script reform from the Qin dynasty to contemporary Unicode debates. EnJoe's stories stage conflicts between inclusion and exclusion—what counts as an encodable character, which graphic forms are discarded, and how these decisions constrain or enable writers working with Sinographs, kana, and their visual and expressive possibilities. By dramatizing everything from Qin-era script reforms to rebellious furigana and proliferating variant characters, EnJoe makes visible the technical infrastructures that underwrite the process of writing. In doing so, the article argues, he exploits the Japanese writing system's capacity for orthographical variation at the limits of possibility. Unicode functions simultaneously as a tool of global standardization and a platform that “standardizes the nonstandard,” with significant consequences for how the humanities preserve, classify, and imagine written forms, and EnJoe's work offers a key case for understanding how script technologies condition literary creativity across languages and periods.

Multiple Diplomatic Centers
abstract: Diplomatic interactions between Japanese Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu and Ming emperor Zhu Di, together with the Ming-Japanese tally trade, have received lively scholarly discussion. This article examines a period before the tally trade momentarily became the major diplomatic channel in Sino-Japanese exchanges. By cross-referencing and comparing sources from China and Japan, the author highlights how various players such as Zhu Yuanzhang, Buddhist monks, Prince Kaneyoshi, Go-Enyū tennō, and Kyushu warrior leaders participated in overseas exchanges. The author argues that the lively diplomatic exchanges between Kyushu and China confirm the existence of multiple diplomatic centers beyond Kyoto. The author proposes seeing Ming's rulership in this light and rethinking it in a broader East Asian context. In particular, Zhu Yuanzhang's flexible policies and careful examination of overseas envoys demonstrate that early Ming's overseas policies cannot be summarized simply as conservative and inward-looking. Instead, they show a high degree of openness and variation in the conduct of overseas affairs. By comparing diplomatic exchanges written in different languages and from different sides, the author argues for the need to move beyond political and territorial boundaries to consider important concepts such as rulership, empire, and imperial order in a connected and transregional perspective.

title: From Click to Boom: The Political Economy of E-Commerce in China
Correlating Race and Caste in Colonial Burma
abstract: Scholars have made clear the impact of colonial governance on modern states’ racial, ethnic, and national identities. Colonial census efforts were a crucial tool in the creation and politicization of such identity categories. This article analyzes “race” definitions and classifications in the colonial censuses of British India from 1872 to 1931 to show how the challenges of defining race in Burma emerged, in part, because of the stepwise colonization of Burma through British India. Specifically, this article asks: What influenced the definitions of race in Burma? How were efforts at developing and understanding a racial schema in Burma shaped by the colonial landscape in which it was embedded? The article argues that colonial ideas about race in Burma developed out of an initial stage of racial classification and knowledge production in India, revealing the complexity of defining race under the influence of both European perceptions of racial difference and local perceptions of social boundaries in India. This article contributes to knowledge of how the creation and implementation of race categories and definitions is a process embedded in a web of colonial structures that extend beyond the colony-colonizer relationship.

title: Push-Car Railways, Camphor, and Coal in the Imperial Hinterland
abstract: This article examines the push-car railway industry in colonial Taiwan from 1895 to the 1930s. It argues that this human-powered transportation resolved a colonial dilemma between the colonial government's economic ambition and its limited capacities as shaped by Taiwan's environmental and colonial conditions. The push-car railways effectively connected Taiwan's local economy to the global market. The article rethinks the relationship between the environment, capitalism, and colonialism from three perspectives. First, muscle-powered technology was crucial to the rise of fossil capitalism at the turn of the century. Second, the push-car railway industry revealed a multilayered relationship between the colonizer and the colonized, profoundly reshaping the environment of the imperial hinterland. Third, as an integral part of fossil capitalism, the push-car railway industry amplified and complicated human cost instead of decreasing it. This analysis unravels how local Taiwanese business actors developed networks under colonial constraints, reshaping socioeconomic and environmental relationships in Taiwan's hinterlands.

Meritocracy Divide
abstract: As a postscript to the collected articles in this forum, this article first discusses how and why a high-stakes test-based admissions system has historically been established in East Asia, contextualizing meritocratic educational selection within the historical experience of “catch-up modernization.” Second, using a theoretical framework of “compressed” modernity and development, it discusses how broader and more recent societal changes have contributed to the development of a high-stakes admissions system. Third, it discusses the implications of these recent changes in admissions for understanding changes in meritocracy. Finally, it describes the problems these rapid and simultaneous changes in admissions and other social spheres have created and what implications these changes have for our understanding of meritocracy in the region. It concludes by discussing how meritocracy has created a new social divide, representing a duality in meritocratic college admissions consisting of traditional high-stakes tests and newly introduced admissions procedures that are more holistic.

College Admission in South Korea
abstract: South Korea is known for its intense focus on education, and college admission in the country has been central to citizens’ sense of fairness. Citizens strongly believe in procedural justice, which is guaranteed by transparent and objective selection schemes based on the one-shot exam called Suneung. However, as a result of a few decades of college admission reforms, such an exam is no longer the primary route to university today. Against this background, this study explores how Korean college students understand fairness as they navigate “meritocratic” selection processes for prestigious universities.

abstract: This essay investigates what it means for young people in East Asia to go to college by looking at the growing number of young adults who attend higher education using National Student Loans. In-depth interviews with nineteen low-income young adults in South Korea and Japan revealed that the decision to attend college has become more common in both societies, with positive evaluations of National Student Loans and student debts. They strategically positioned their student loans by distinguishing them from other loans. In addition, the author found that higher education has more complex meanings in East Asia than simply a means of economic benefit. For example, in South Korea, higher education was equated with gaining prestige goods, while in Japan, going to college was considered the ideal way for young people to spend their twenties.

title: Out with the Old, In with the New
abstract: Research on meritocracy often assumes equal weighting of different types of merit, overlooking how people assign relative power to them in justifying social superiority. This study, based on sixty-two interviews, examines how educators and students navigate Taiwan's dual-merit admissions system, where traditional test scores intersect with a new holistic screening model. The author finds that students continue to treat test scores as primary markers of success, while professors and teachers increasingly prioritize nontest merit as signals of social distinction. This divergence highlights varying rates of adaptation to Taiwan's dual-merit system, exposing tensions between old and new standards. These findings shed light on how merit is perceived and operationalized amid institutional transformation, and they contribute to broader debates on fairness and legitimacy in East Asian educational systems.

title: Therapy, Spirituality, and East Asian Imaginaries
The Narrowing Sea: Fukuoka, Pusan, and the Rise and Fall of an Imperial Region
The Price of Freedom: Lèse-majesté Prosecutions and the Politics of Bail in Thailand
abstract: In recent years, Thai courts have arbitrarily used the lèse majesté law to prosecute hundreds of defendants. This use of lèse majesté has been an important part of a reaction against a movement that had been mobilised nationwide during 2020–2021 calling for reform of politics. Breaking the kingdom’s biggest taboo, the movement explicitly criticised the monarchy and called for monarchy reform. Besides an unprecedented number of cases, what distinguishes the recent wave of persecutions is the way the court handles the question of bail. In the past, almost all lèse majesté defendants were likely to be imprisoned from an early stage of investigation, and they were constantly denied bail. Recently, however, granting bail has been more common. This research examines the politics of bail in lèse majesté cases, arguing that the trend of granting bail should be considered a political tactic of the courts while maintaining the prosecution of disloyal subjects. Setting bail so high means ordinary people cannot reach it. Despite this high price for freedom, the monarchy reform movement and several civic associations manage to secure bail for most defendants. This article examines fundraising role as a form of resistance against the power of the court and the crown.

title: Digital Defiance: Analysis of Public Responses to Youth Activism in Thailand, 2020–2023
abstract: During Thailand’s 2020–2023 wave of youth activism, once unsayable political topics moved into online debate, pushing the boundaries of public discourse. Anchored in the concept of Thai-Style Democracy, this article examines how discourse on Twitter/X shapes what becomes sayable, respectable, or sanctionable. The article argues that platformed talk did not merely reflect opinion but recalibrated legitimacy under Thai-Style Democracy. Using Critical Discourse Analysis of 4,705 tweets, five recurrent patterns were identified: (i) self-identification and labelling; (ii) rights, freedoms, and duties framed through a duty-first moral order; (iii) guardianist legitimacy and platform scaling; (iv) karmic idioms as moral justifications; and (v) conditional support and opposition tied to compatibility with duty and non-violation of royal authority. Together, these dynamics illuminated a paradox: expanding speakability around monarchy reform alongside a narrowing acceptability of youth activism. The analysis shows how online discourse participated in legitimating institutional responses and reshaping horizons of action. This study contributes to broader discussions of digital activism, generational conflict, and the resilience of Thai-Style Democracy under democratic pressure by linking the nuanced dynamics of online discourse to political events.

title: Illicit Parallel Trading, State Permission, and Legality: A Comparative Analysis in the Southern Chinese Seaboard
authors: Lawrence Ka-ki Ho; KuoRay Mao; Henry Hin-Yan Chan; Alexander Hagan
abstract: This article applies institutional and media content analysis to investigate the legitimation and criminalisation of cross-border trade within the "Southern Chinese Seaboard," specifically between Taiwan and China and between Hong Kong and mainland China, a region characterised by diverse taxation and legal jurisdictions, as well as rapidly evolving political-economic and regional geo-political dynamics. This study re-evaluates common media portrayals and simplistic perceptions of "illicit" and "parallel trading" as merely spontaneous actions by individuals embedded in criminal networks. Instead, we posit that such activities stem from deliberately vague taxation and legal definitions, as well as enforcement strategies resulting from collusion between state and non-state actors. Utilising the "Regime of Permission" framework, this study examines how political actors manipulate the definitions of licit and illicit trading to achieve political objectives, thereby creating loopholes that non-state actors exploit. The findings demonstrate that the delineation and oversight of illicit trade have evolved in response to shifting economic relationships and the development of enforcement institutions within a changing geo-political landscape, offering deeper insight into the state's role in creating and maintaining liminal spaces that regulate the boundaries between lawful, unlawful, and socially illicit trade.

title: Banditry in the Sundarbans: The Political Economy of a Mangrove Frontier
authors: Md. Tanvir Mahtab; M. Anwar Hossen; Md. Shihabul Islam
abstract: This study examines the political economy of forest-centred banditry in the Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest, where the Ganges, Brahmaputra, and Meghna rivers meet. It focuses on the roles played by patronage networks in banditry. Employing a qualitative and case study approach, the research seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of the political economy of forest-centred banditry. The interviews were conducted in the Mongla and Rampal areas of Bagerhat district, Bangladesh. Findings reveal a deeply entrenched system of exploitation and control. Local business elites (mahajans) and political actors exploit individuals through the dadni debt system and political manipulation, coercing them into banditry. This system is sustained through hierarchical structures led by boro bhai (big brother figures) and enforced by violence. Bandits abduct fishermen for ransom, with local politicians acting as intermediaries, collecting significant amounts annually. Businessmen support bandit gangs to monopolise natural resources, resulting in fierce competition among traders. Additionally, powerful figures profit from illegal enterprises such as the arms trade and prostitution. Further, the study identifies a deep relationship between bandits and local government officials, highlighting systemic corruption through monthly payments for protection and information.

title: Unequal Chains: Global Value Chains and Income Disparity
authors: Kay Kiang Tan; Andrew Jia Yi Kam; M. Niaz Asadullah
abstract: As countries deepen their integration into global value chains (GVCs) to pursue industrial growth and economic advancement, a critical question remains unresolved: Who truly benefits from this participation? This study examines the effects of GVC participation on income disparities within the manufacturing sector. Three measures of income inequality are employed – value-added distribution, wage distribution, and labour income share – based on the World Bank Economic Enterprise Survey data for 44 countries and 16 manufacturing industries between 2006 and 2016. The results reveal that the choice of inequality measure is crucial. GVC participation reduces income inequality in value-added and wage distribution but increases inequality in labour income share. At the country level, backward and forward linkages reduce income inequality in lower-income economies, while effects are not significant in upper-middle- and high-income countries. Regionally, Asia shows more equitable value-added through backward linkages and equitable wages through overall GVC and forward linkages. However, overall GVC participation and forward linkages are also associated with a decline in labour income share, suggesting that while GVC integration may improve wage equality, the proportion of value-added accruing to labour tends to shrink.

title: Indonesia’s Illiberal Capitalism and the 2025 Protests: A Reply to Wijaya and Jayasuriya
abstract: Indonesia was less affected by the 2008 global crisis than many developed capitalist economies, but can it be said to have followed a similar path, leading to austerity that deepens disincorporation of the subordinate classes and the decline of liberal democracy as a source of legitimacy for capitalism? Wijaya and Jayasuriya suggest so. However, it cannot be forgotten that Indonesia’s capitalism has long relied on an illiberal political-legal order as a means of accumulation and legitimacy, despite post-1998 democratisation. This arrangement persists because there is neither a coherent progressive movement capable of shifting the balance of power nor a rupture within the capitalist fractions that introduces a new way to sustain bourgeois hegemony. Hence, characterising Indonesia as evolving towards Poulantzas’s model of authoritarian statism overlooks the specificity of the mode of capitalist accumulation. What has happened in Indonesia is the deepening of the already illiberal mode, often provoking mass protests. However, this new direction is not the result of a post-crisis re-organisation of capital but rather arises from the logic of accumulation in which sections of oligarchic alliance seek to further concentrate power and wealth in the absence of the organised left.

title: State, Capital, and the Crisis of Social Reproduction in Indonesia: A Rejoinder
abstract: This rejoinder to Mudhoffir (Citation2026) identifies three key theoretical points of disagreement in the response to our commentary on Indonesian protests of 2025 (Wijaya and Jayasuriya Citation2026). First, the “authoritarian continuity thesis” advanced by our critics misses the way in which the “rule of capital” is organised within the state apparatus. The response to our article rests on an instrumentalist reading of the Indonesian state, which is contrasted to a more structural understanding set out in our 2026 commentary. Second, this perspective enables a better comprehension of the shifts in the form of authoritarian political regimes in response to a variety of often overlapping crises. Third, protests must be understood not simply as a set of grievances about elite impunity but signify a fundamental shift in the structure of the working or labouring class, which is itself the product of capitalist transformation over the last decades. Here, it is contended that these conflicts now find expression in new forms of politics over access to means of social reproduction.

title: Invisible Brokers, Visible Haze: Value Chains and the Political Ecology of Northern Thailand’s Maize Economy
abstract: Each dry season, thick haze blankets northern Thailand. Maize cultivation, driven largely by demand for animal feed, is one of its most politically contested sources. Policy responses often target farmers through burning bans, technical fixes, and behavioural change campaigns. This article focuses on the middlemen who link upland maize fields to downstream feed markets. It shows that brokers, traders, and silo operators, by controlling access to credit, logistics, and markets, translate corporate demand, price volatility, and regulatory pressures into everyday farming practices. Moral economies of debt, reciprocity, and patronage intersect with buyer-driven value chain pressures to shape brokerage practices and disperse accountability for environmental harm. These practices reinforce farmers’ dependence on maize, and make burning appear the most viable option while displacing responsibility onto farmers and shielding large agribusinesses. The article demonstrates that market power operates through everyday social relations of credit, trust, and loyalty to reproduce unequal commodity relations. This helps explain why haze persists despite repeated policy interventions. The article integrates middlemen into environmental governance analyses, shows that value chain governance and moral economy combine to reproduce environmental injustice, and contributes to meatways scholarship, tracing the intermediary networks through which national and regional meat demand reproduces environmental harm.

title: The Contours Of Working-Class Debt: Precarity, Gender, And Labour Discipline In Cambodia’s Construction Sector
abstract: This article argues that in Cambodia’s construction sector, overall levels of precarity play a key role in shaping the extent to which debt functions as a mechanism of labour discipline. Building on LeBaron’s reconceptualisation of debt bondage as a class-based form of labour discipline, it situates worker indebtedness within the broader structural conditions through which it acquires coercive force. Drawing on data collected from 600 workers employed in cement factories and on construction sites, the article reveals that debt’s coercive power stems less from its absolute burden than from its interaction with employment precarity. Although workers in both sub-sectors faced significant indebtedness, cement factory workers benefited from relatively stable employment, monthly wages, and access to social security, whereas construction workers were paid irregularly, experienced wage theft, and were excluded from social protection. These dynamics operated in profoundly gendered ways, reflecting women’s household financial responsibilities and difficulties securing formal credit. By foregrounding the relationship between indebtedness and structural precarity, the article argues that it is the configuration of precarity itself that determines the depth of debt-based coercion in contemporary Cambodia.

title: A Businesswoman in Meiji Japan
abstract: Women are conspicuously underexamined in the business and economic histories of modern Japan. Although wives and widows played central roles in the financial management of their families and family businesses, they have typically remained hidden behind the names and accomplishments of their more visible male relations. This was true not only in Japan but also in other countries undergoing rapid industrialization in the long nineteenth century. Some women, however, did leave traces of their economic activity and leadership. As scholars encounter more and more of these so-called anomalies, the need grows for new, more inclusive historical narratives that can account for their existence and impacts. This article responds by studying the involvement of one especially visible married businesswoman in the development of her marital family’s coal mine in Kyushu’s Chikuhō region. More specifically we investigate the networking and management approaches of Hirooka Asako (1849–1919) and contextualize them with those of female business leaders working in male-dominated industries in and beyond Japan. Unexamined or understudied contracts, financial records, speeches, interviews, and editorials as well as private, unofficial sources like correspondence, memoirs, and eulogies reveal that she played a leading role in Uruno Mine’s development and management. Mobilizing determination, familial and professional networks with men, and direct management strategies, she personally oversaw the metamorphosis of this failing project into a successful, profitable enterprise. Her methods and achievements in fact resemble those of prewar modern Japan’s few famous businesswomen, of a few well-known Western women entrepreneurs, and, likely, of many less visible women. If, as we demonstrate, dynamic, enterprising women were active entrepreneurs, respected collaborators of men, and influential contributors to Japan’s economic and industrial development during the Meiji period (1868–1912), the inclusion of their stories can complicate scholars’ understanding of Japanese business and economic history.

title: The Hearts of People in the World
abstract: This article explores the economic dimensions of the late fiction of the seventeenth-century writer Ihara Saikaku, asking how the author’s understanding of the marketplace shaped his humanistic studies of “the hearts of people” (hito-gokoro). Applying methods of economic criticism to the posthumous Tying Off Saikaku’s Loose Ends (Saikaku oridome, 1694), I argue that the author’s late writings develop a formal homology between the imperfect rationality of the early market economy and the ineffable dynamism of the human heart.

title: Grounding Empire Through Burial Grounds
abstract: This article examines how the Japanese military, notably the Kwantung Army, used the acquisition and maintenance of military burial grounds to challenge Chinese sovereignty in Manchuria (currently Northeast China) and expand Japan’s territorial control in seemingly “peaceful” periods. The burial grounds became contested sites where debates over sovereignty and different groups’ claims of land use played out. With a close focus on the military-use land, this article challenges the previous depiction of Japanese imperialism in Manchuria as informal imperialism and enriches our understanding of how the military reshaped social and political relationships in the empire through the control of land. This article also enriches historical writing on the Kwantung Army, which tends to focus on its military roles. The Kwantung Army in Manchuria not only enacted its power through military actions but also far more extensively penetrated Manchuria’s local communities even before the Manchukuo era (1932–45).

title: To the Virtuous Go the Spoils
abstract: This article examines Taiheiki (Chronicle of Great Peace, fourteenth century) as a critical intervention in medieval Japanese historiography. It challenges conventional court-versus-rebel binaries, framing the fragmentation of authority during the Nanbokuchō age through Neo-Confucian concepts of virtue, such as the three bonds and five virtues, the Mandate of Heaven, and revolutionary reign change. Figures like Emperor Go-Daigo and his loyal general Kusunoki Masashige expose the erosion of imperial legitimacy through failed moral governance. Taiheiki offers a flexible, genre-defying model of historical change, challenging myths of imperial inviolability and anticipating early modern re-conceptualizations of virtue, sovereignty, and political order.

title: Ainu Handicrafts
abstract: This article examines the mass commercialization of Ainu handicrafts as Hokkaido’s official folk art and signature souvenir during the 1930s. Focusing on the political economy of these works, it analyzes how the Japanese empire constructed a colonial handicraft industry that promoted the popular consumption of Ainu woodcarvings and attus textiles as symbols of Japan’s civilizing mission over the Ainu people. Despite such appropriation, Ainu craftspeople repurposed these works as instruments of political mobilization to confront colonial inequalities. At Asahikawa, Ainu activists from the Third Chikabumi Land Dispute envisioned collective handicraft workshops as a centerpiece of their proposal to dismantle their reservation and construct a new village. In the Saru River basin, Ainu weavers also drew on community-based management of mountain forests to connect attus textile production to Indigenous land rights. By tracing Ainu cultural production across these sites, the article argues that Ainu handicrafts were critical sites for the articulation of Ainu demands for land recovery, local autonomy, and equitable resource use.

title: Acting Like Female Spirit Mediums
abstract: In 1913, Nakachi Kamado called for a public trial in Naha, Okinawa, to contest the accusation that she had acted as a yuta, or female spirit medium. The trial captivated city residents, drawing hundreds to the courtroom and even more to commercial theaters featuring plays about the trial. This article argues that the trial and plays articulated tensions of class and gender pulsating through the city of Naha. From police surveillance to the dispossession of the former ruling class and an influx of working-class women, tensions wrought by Japanese colonialism and urbanization found powerful expression in the trial and plays.

title: Introduction to the Special Issue: Crossing Boundaries in Modern Korean Literature and Culture
Negotiating the Colonial Dilemma Through Science Fiction: Translating Jules Verne in Early Twentieth-Century Colonial Korea
abstract: This article examines the emergence of science fiction (SF) in early twentieth-century Korea by analyzing the first two Korean translations of Jules Verne—Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1907–8) and The Begum’s Fortune (1908). It argues that these relay translations, produced during the years between the Russo-Japanese War and formal Japanese annexation, reveal how Korean intellectuals navigated what the article terms the “colonial dilemma”: the challenge of rethinking national identity amid accelerated modernization and encroaching imperial domination. Rather than passively importing European SF, Korean translators actively reshaped the texts through genre relabeling, annotation, and selective adaptation, using them simultaneously as vehicles of scientific enlightenment and as tools for articulating Korea’s precarious place within global geopolitics. The article further contends that the early Korean use of the term “science fiction”—predating its standardization in the Anglophone world—calls for a reconsideration of global SF timelines and assumptions about the genre’s origins. By situating Korean SF within the broader East Asian circulation of Verne’s works and by highlighting the translators’ interventions into colonialist narratives, this study demonstrates that SF in Korea emerged not as an extension of European imperial imagination but through a complex interplay of colonial, anti-colonial, and nation-building impulses.

title: Translated Poetry in Younghill Kang’s The Grass Roof and the Tradition of Inset Poetry in Premodern Korean Fiction
abstract: Younghill Kang’s 1931 novel The Grass Roof, long taken as the first commercially successful novel by a Korean in English, is unusual for incorporating sixty-five of its author’s translations of East Asian poetry into its narrative fabric. These embedded translations represented one of the early mass audiences for Korean poetry in English. This article argues that The Grass Roof adapts the literary convention of inset poetry (sabipsi) from the premodern Korean novel, hybridizing it with English-language autobiographical fiction. It proves Kang knew traditional narrative models by analyzing his depictions in the novel of the Kuunmong and Ch’unhyang chŏn. It then examines two different uses of inset poetry in the novel: (1) retrospective ornamentation by the narrator and (2) dynamic plot advancement by characters. The second function, in particular, reflects classical uses of sabipsi to heighten scenes of courtship and erudition. Kang’s use of inset poetry gave Korean poetry an unusually early global audience at the same time as it drew Western and Korean novelistic techniques together in a new, shared experiment.

title: Reading O Changhwan Translating Sergey Esenin in Seoul, 1946
abstract: This article explores the allegorical layers of meaning that emerge from one translator-poet partnership in the aftermath of the collapse of the Japanese empire in Korea. The iconoclastic modernist poet O Changhwan’s first published book in a newly liberated Korea was a translation of poems by the deceased Russian poet Sergey Esenin. O was translating at a moment when the Korean language was returning to public life after suppression under colonial rule and amid escalating violence on the partitioned peninsula. Reading O’s translations and lengthy afterword opens a window onto the scene of Seoul in 1946, one year before O was to cross over the thirty-eighth parallel into the northern zone. With the aim of rethinking the creative legacies of the early Cold War, this article explores the many meanings created in and through O’s translation.

title: Milan Kundera’s Poetry in North Korea and Socialist World Literature in the 1950s
abstract: This essay examines Milan Kundera’s unexpected presence in 1950s North Korean literature, revealing a forgotten chapter of socialist world literature in the Cold War era. The study focuses on three of Kundera’s poems related to the Korean War: “The Gardener,” “Korean Ballad,” and his epic poem “The Last May,” which revolves around the anti-fascist martyr Julius Fučík. By analyzing North Korean literary journals including Chosŏn munhak, the essay traces how Kundera’s early socialist poetry arrived in North Korea as part of broader international solidarity efforts during and after the Korean War. Noting how the translation of these works occurred at a specific historical moment when North Korea was actively engaging with Eastern European literature before turning inward in the 1960s, the essay situates Kundera within North Korea’s evolving conception of “world literature,” which shifted from Soviet-centeredness through Eastern European engagement to eventual interest in the Tricontinental (Asia, Africa, Latin America) before closing off entirely. The divided reception exemplifies the broader fragmentation of world literature during the Cold War, gesturing to the power dynamic that shapes literary histories in conversation with but also beyond ideological boundaries.

title: Interpretive Praxis Under Pax Americana: Paik Nak-chung’s Reading of D.H. Lawrence in 1980s South Korea
abstract: This article examines Paik Nak-chung’s (Paek Nakch’ŏng’s) 1982 translation and reading of D.H. Lawrence’s Studies in Classic American Literature (1923) as a case of interpretive praxis under Cold War authoritarianism in South Korea. Situated between the aftershocks of the Kwangju Uprising and the intensification of anti-American student activism, Paik’s essay “The American Dream and the Burden of American Literature” appears, at first glance, anomalous: Why would a leading critic of literary engagement turn to Lawrence at a moment when dissident reading communities centered on Marx, Fanon, and other banned revolutionary texts? I argue that Paik’s sustained engagement with Lawrence is best understood as a metacritical strategy that converts reading and translation into a political intervention. Working through Lawrence’s symptomatic critique of “American democracy” and the ideological work of the American dream, Paik exposes US imperial duplicity while simultaneously resisting the nativist essentialism that could accompany virulent anti-Americanism in 1980s Korea. Lawrence’s insistence on stripping “democratic and idealistic clothes” from American utterance becomes, in Paik’s hands, a method for historicizing—one that links the contradictions of American nation-building to South Korea’s compressed modernization and US-backed authoritarianism. Tracing how Paik reframes Lawrence’s critique of the “whole soul” of America, I show how he articulates a decolonizing stance that resists simple binaries of foreign imperialist versus authentic minjung. Finally, situating Paik’s Lawrence within a longer genealogy of criticism shaped by Matthew Arnold and F. R. Leavis, I argue that Paik’s “double project of modernity” (ijung kwajeron) marks a commitment to hold aesthetic autonomy and political praxis in productive tension with each other.

title: Archaeological Translation: How to Translate Diasporic Korean Literature
abstract: Min Jin Lee’s Pachinko chronicles four generations of Zainichi (Koreans in Japan) from the colonial era to the 1980s. Its translation process remains enigmatic; Lee imagined the narrative in Korean and Japanese before writing the novel in English. Consequently, the English original and its two Korean translated versions produce divergent meanings. This article investigates the translational issues in the two Korean versions, questioning the hierarchical order between the original Anglophone text and its translations. Building upon postcolonial translation scholarship, we first examine restored dialects in the Korean versions that are absent in the English text, analyzing their intersection with discourses of class, gender, and ethnicity. Second, we compare the opening sentences of the three versions, unearthing distinct insights into colonial and postcolonial histories embedded within each text. By unsettling conventional notions of originality, this comparative analysis introduces a new framework termed “archaeological translation.” Through this lens, we critique Lee’s mode of representation that flattens cultural and historical specificity, while demonstrating how translated versions evolve into distinctive texts with their own historical, political, and cultural perspectives in the transnational age.

title: The Magical Agency of Parameters as Intent and Meaning: The Translation Application in Decision to Leave
abstract: This essay examines how the translation application in Park Chan-wook’s Heŏjil kyŏlsim (Decision to Leave, 2022) functions as a narrative agent and framework for parametric mediation. Semantic entropy designates information loss when neural translation compresses multivalent meanings into probable outputs; yet this entropy proves generatively productive, creating new possibilities in gaps between languages. Close readings examine scenes where the app mistranslates Chinese into Korean, transforming affective complexity into anatomical literalism, imposing unwarranted honorifics, and reducing Confucian ethics to suit consumer preferences. The screenwriters deliberately crafted these failures; paradoxically, such errors generate meanings exceeding both languages. Drawing on Walter Benjamin, Susan Bassnett, and neural translation research, this study shows how mistranslations illuminate both limitations and generative capacities in algorithmic and human understanding. These insufficiencies become narratively productive through a hermeneutics of irresolution: an interpretive mode refusing closure, locating meaning in interstices between competing translations. Characterizing this dynamic as parametric creativity, I argue that Decision to Leave transforms technical constraints into aesthetic method. As artificial intelligence increasingly mediates communication, the film reminds us of interstices arising from encounters between disparate entities: the tremor in voices, the weight of pauses, and the irreducible difference between heart as an organ and heart as feeling.

title: Between Eco-Governmentality and Forest Management Cooperatives: Reinterpreting South Korean Reforestation in the 1970s and 1980s from the Local Level
abstract: In 1973, the Park Chung Hee government launched its first Reforestation Plan to deal with the pressing issues surrounding forest loss, soil erosion, and forest management through countrywide tree planting and stricter control of forest use for logging. The top-down campaigns, often referred to as a “green Yushin,” can be understood as eco-governmentality with direct state intervention in the sylvan environment. However, to recognize the effects of reforestation on the local level, there is a need for further consideration of the role of forest owners. The West German and South Korean governments promoted the establishment of Forest Management Cooperatives (FMCs). After their introduction in Ulju County, the model was subsequently transferred to other regions all over the country throughout the 1980s. The cooperatives contributed to the economic livelihood of the rural population and enabled the transfer of forest management skills and practices to forest owners amid the government-led campaign. The forest owners could then actively participate in decision-making processes on the local level. This article proposes a new understanding of the reforestation campaigns that took place under the authoritarian government by engaging perspectives from the local level and introducing the new models of cooperatives that were carried out as rural development projects.

title: Cleared for Takeoff: The Economic and Environmental History of Incheon International Airport in 1990s South Korea
abstract: In 1990, the South Korean government announced the construction of a new international airport on reclaimed land to the west of Seoul. This proposal drew the ire of environmental groups and major newspapers as an environmental and economic disaster. The international airport construction proposal arrived at an inflection point of post-1987 democratization, government liberalization of travel restrictions, the growth of the aviation industry, rising environmentalism, and the beginning of a global recession. While large-scale infrastructure projects had enabled South Korea’s rapid economic rise, the high environmental costs sparked intense public interest among South Koreans. However, the openness of the post-1987 period was a double-edged sword for environmental groups. While they found greater freedom to organize and high public interest in environmental issues, the public also had the freedom to decide the type of environmentalism and lifestyle they wanted to pursue. This article examines the Incheon International Airport construction proposal as a case study of the intersection between economic history and environmental history, with popular sentiment as a key swing variable. This study argues that the Incheon airport proposal illustrates the contemporary nature of South Korean environmentalism, lifestyle objectives, and economic consciousness.

experiences of tension, difference and contestation.For nearly four decades, efforts to transcend the epistemological borders, heuristics, and categories associated with an earlier imagining of Southeast Asia (that sought to delineate it as a distinctive, coherent and legitimate unit of analysis) continues to exemplify emergent research.Reconfiguring Southeast Asia by problematising and
